sections.heading: Session length, session frequency, and what each one buys
paragraphs: Parents usually ask about price per hour and rarely about the shape of the hour, which is the wrong way round. The same total spend produces very different results depending on how it is divided. Two 60-minute sessions a week beat one 120-minute session for almost every student under sixteen, because retention depends on the gap between exposures rather than on time in the chair. Above sixteen, and particularly for subjects that require sustained written output, the longer block starts to win.

The table below sets out what each shape actually achieves. Read the last column carefully, because it names what the format cannot do. A 45-minute session cannot hold a full timed paper and a review of it. A single weekly 60-minute session cannot keep a student ahead in two subjects. A four-hour weekend block cannot be absorbed by a thirteen-year-old no matter how it is presented. Matching the shape to the task is free; getting it wrong costs a term.

Frequency interacts with the calendar. Through the teaching term, one session a week per subject is usually right, because the limiting factor is what the class has covered. In the final phase before a series, the limiting factor becomes how many papers the student can sit and have marked, which makes two or three sessions the sensible number. Going above three rarely helps, because the student needs unsupervised hours to do the work the sessions set.

There is one exception worth naming. A student whose problem is a specific decaying method - reacting masses, logarithms, a particular proof technique - benefits from three short sessions in one week and then nothing for a fortnight. Spacing designed around the method rather than around the calendar is unusual to buy and genuinely more efficient, and it is easier to arrange when no journey is involved.

sections.heading: The mandatory UAE subjects sitting on top of your child's timetable
paragraphs: Families choosing a school on curriculum alone are sometimes surprised by the subject load in the first term, and the reason is federal rather than local. UAE private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but they must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. That is why Arabic and Social Studies appear on a British or IB timetable alongside everything the board requires, and why they consume hours a parent had not budgeted for.

The clearest published detail on how these subjects are timetabled comes from Dubai's regulator, and it is worth reading even for a Sharjah family because it shows the mechanics. KHDA calculates mandatory-subject instructional time on a 40-minute lesson unit, allows schools to vary lesson length provided the total weekly time is met, and advises that any mandatory-subject lesson should run at least 25 minutes. It also requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and states that combined classes are strictly prohibited.

Two consequences follow for tutoring. First, first-language Arabic and additional-language Arabic are genuinely different courses with different expectations, so the tutor has to match the stream your child sits rather than the subject name on the report. Second, the content is tightly controlled: KHDA states that for these subjects the use of any different or additional content, without prior permission from the Ministry, is strictly prohibited. Tutoring here means supporting the school's own material, not supplying an alternative syllabus.

In practice this is a small weekly commitment that prevents a predictable problem. A student carrying a weak Arabic grade through to the end of school discovers at the equivalency stage that it was never counted among the five required subjects anyway, but still arrives at a report card conversation every term. Thirty to forty-five minutes a week, on the school's own material, usually settles it.

sections.heading: What a tutor may do with coursework, and what nobody may do
paragraphs: Scheduling questions aside, the single most important boundary on this page is the one around assessed work. Internal Assessments, the Extended Essay, the Theory of Knowledge essay and the MYP Personal Project must be the student's own work, and the student signs a declaration confirming it. Any provider offering to supply finished assessed work is offering something that puts the candidate at risk of a malpractice finding, and at least one page competing for these searches sells exactly that.

Legitimate support is narrower and, done properly, more valuable. A tutor can teach the underlying content, translate each assessment criterion into plain language, help a student narrow a research question until it is answerable inside the word limit, challenge whether a claim in a draft is actually supported by the data, point out that a results table has no uncertainty treatment, and read a draft against the published criteria and name the weak criterion. All of that is teaching and all of it is allowed.

What a tutor may not do is author any part of the submission: not a paragraph, not a methodology, not a rewritten conclusion, not a set of results. We tell students at the start of any supervision block that anything they did not write has to come out before submission. We also do not reproduce or distribute board syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes or grade-boundary tables; we reference the official source and work from material the student legitimately holds through school.

The scheduling point worth adding is that supervision hours and teaching hours are not interchangeable. A DP2 student in a deadline week needs a session that reads and questions their own draft, not one that teaches new content. Planning the year so those weeks are protected for supervision is the difference between coursework that is finished early and coursework that is finished at midnight.

sections.heading: What tutoring costs in this market, and what moves the number
paragraphs: Three of the six pages competing for these searches publish no price at all, and the two that do quote in US dollars. The table below gives the published AED bands for the UAE market as read in October 2026, with the source named in each row, alongside the scheduling factor that moves the figure. These are market rates rather than an IB Gram price list, and nothing here is a quote for your child.

The scheduling column is the part that is specific to this page. Session length changes the effective hourly cost, because a 90-minute booking is normally priced below two 60-minute ones. Frequency changes it too: an intensive phase of two or three sessions a week is the most expensive month of the year and should therefore be the shortest. Time of day matters less than parents expect online, and matters a great deal for in-home arrangements, where a late slot at the end of a tutor's route costs more than a mid-afternoon one.

The figure nobody quotes is the number of hours. A correctly diagnosed technique problem can resolve in eight to ten sessions. The same student with a tutor re-teaching content they already knew can absorb forty and finish in the same place. That is why this page keeps returning to diagnosis: it is the only variable that changes the total by a factor of four. Ask any provider what the hours are for before negotiating what they cost.

IB Gram does not publish a fixed rate card here, because the number depends on subject, level and how much of the work is supervision rather than teaching. A short consultation gives you the band before you commit to anything, and we will tell you if the honest answer is fewer hours than you expected.

sections.heading: Getting started without buying the wrong thing
paragraphs: The first conversation should establish three things: which subject and syllabus, when your child is genuinely available, and what the last two pieces of marked work say. The third matters most and is the one parents most often skip. A marked paper tells a tutor in five minutes which component the marks are leaving from, and that is frequently not where the student thinks it is or where the report card implies.

Then we match a tutor who teaches that exact board and level, and run an introductory session at no charge - one per family, about thirty minutes, with the student present rather than only the parent. The purpose is to test the match before anyone commits to a block. If it is wrong, we change the tutor rather than suggest you give it another week, because a mismatched pairing does not improve with persistence.

If no specialist is free, we say so in that first conversation. For mainstream combinations this is rare. For scarce Higher Level subjects in the weeks right before a written series it does happen, and the wait is usually a week or two. When no UAE-based specialist is available we offer one from our wider pool, which is centred on India; the delivery is identical because it was always online, and the tutor picks up your school's internal deadlines from the student's own documents in the first session.

On timing, the useful moment to start is when a marked piece of work comes back worse than expected, not when the mock results arrive. Eight weeks before a paper there is still time to change the technique that is costing marks. Two weeks before, the only honest offer is help with revision, which is a smaller thing. And if the entry deadline has already passed, the tier your child is sitting is fixed, so the plan has to work inside it.

process.title: Give us the real return time
process.description: Not the school's finishing time but the time your child walks through the door, including the pick-up queue and any activity. Every scheduling decision on this page follows from that number, and an optimistic version of it is the commonest reason a weekly slot starts moving by week three.

process.title: Name the board and level
process.description: Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1 are different papers with different pacing, and the syllabus code sits on your child's exam entry rather than on the textbook. Getting this right in the first message removes the usual cause of a wasted opening session.

process.title: Send two marked pieces of work
process.description: We read them to find which component is losing the marks. That diagnosis decides session length and frequency, which is why it comes before any discussion of how many hours to buy. It usually also shortens the answer.

process.title: Test the match at no charge
process.description: One introductory session per family, roughly thirty minutes, with the student in the room. If the pairing does not work we change the tutor. Bring a recent marked paper, because it makes the half hour considerably more useful than a general conversation.

process.title: Agree the phases, not just the slot
process.description: We set out what the hour is for in the teaching term, during mocks, through Ramadan, in the final phase and across study leave, so the schedule changes on purpose rather than drifting. That is also when we agree what happens to the slot in the weeks the school takes back.

whyPoints.title: Scheduling treated as part of the teaching
whyPoints.description: Session length, frequency and time of day are decided from the student's real day and the job the hour has to do. Most arrangements in this area fail on the clock rather than on subject knowledge, so this is where the planning effort goes first.

whyPoints.title: No travel in the arrangement
whyPoints.description: Lessons run one-to-one over live video, so the Muwaileh dismissal window and the University City traffic never shorten a paid hour or push a start time. That also means a slot can move without a wasted journey, which matters in exam season when school revision sessions appear late.

whyPoints.title: A plan that changes shape with the calendar
whyPoints.description: Mock fortnight, coursework deadline weeks, Ramadan and study leave each need a different kind of session, and two of them need fewer. We write the phases down in advance rather than discovering them, which is why the arrangement survives the spring term.

whyPoints.title: Every figure attributed
whyPoints.description: The AED bands here carry the source that published them and the month they were read. We publish no satisfaction percentages, student counts or ratings, because we cannot produce the underlying data for them.

whyPoints.title: A stated line on coursework
whyPoints.description: Teaching, criterion explanation and feedback on the student's own drafts. No authored paragraphs, no supplied results, no finished submissions, and no redistribution of official papers or mark schemes.

whyPoints.title: Availability stated upfront
whyPoints.description: If a scarce Higher Level subject has a wait this term, we say so in the first conversation and tell you where the alternative tutor is based. A two-week wait you can plan around is manageable; one discovered after payment is not.

faqs.question: What is the earliest a weekday lesson can start for a child living in Al Suyoh?
faqs.answer: For a secondary student at a Muwaileh-cluster school, 17:00 is the honest floor, and 17:45 if there is any after-school activity. Children at schools closer to University City Road, in Al Zahia for instance, can sometimes hold 16:30. The limiting factor is the pick-up queue in the dismissal window rather than the drive itself, which routinely adds fifteen to twenty-five minutes. Because lessons are delivered online, whatever time you choose actually holds, so a realistic later slot works better than an optimistic early one that gets rescheduled every second week.

faqs.question: How long should a session be for a Year 10 student who gets home at six?
faqs.answer: Sixty minutes through the teaching term, moving to ninety in the final eight to twelve weeks before the series. The reason is the job rather than the age: an hour is enough to teach a topic, mark a set of questions and set the next piece of work, but it cannot hold a full timed paper section plus a review of it. If six o'clock is the genuine return time, start at 18:30 once the student has eaten, and put the longer sessions on a weekend morning where concentration is better.

faqs.question: Can lessons move to after Iftar during Ramadan in Sharjah?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for most families that is the better option than pausing for the month. School days usually shorten, the household routine shifts, and a teenager's alert hours move to the evening after Iftar or a quiet stretch in the afternoon. We reschedule the slot for the month on request and move it back afterwards without renegotiation. For a DP2 student the timing matters, because a month away in the middle of coursework season is expensive in a way that is hard to recover from in the spring term.

faqs.question: Does the Sharjah school week affect when tutoring happens?
faqs.answer: It affects it twice. The weekday evening window in this part of the emirate is roughly 17:00 to 20:30 once the school run and dinner are accounted for, and in a household with more than one student that window is shared. Weekend mornings are the least contested hours in the week, because nothing competes with them, which makes them the right home for primary and lower-MYP students and for any long analytical session. We usually build a plan that uses both rather than forcing everything into weekday evenings.

faqs.question: Is a 90-minute session better value than two 60-minute ones?
faqs.answer: It depends on the student's age and the task. Below about sixteen, two shorter sessions almost always win, because retention depends on the gap between exposures more than on time in the chair. Above sixteen, and for subjects needing sustained written output such as English A Paper 1 or Analysis and Approaches Paper 3, the longer block wins because the student can read, plan, write and be marked inside one session. A 90-minute booking is also usually priced below two separate hours, so cost follows the same split.

faqs.question: We have two children at different schools in Muwaileh. Can the slots run back to back?
faqs.answer: Yes, and staggering them is usually better than running them simultaneously. A common shape here is 17:00 for the younger child and 18:30 for the older one, which gives both a sensible time without the household having to manage two sessions at once. Because the tutors are different specialists working online, there is no constraint about one person being in two places. The thing to guard against is the exam-year sibling gradually absorbing both slots, which is the single commonest failure in multi-child households in this area.

faqs.question: Does Al Suyoh have any IB schools of its own?
faqs.answer: Al Suyoh is primarily residential, and students here travel to schools in Muwaileh, University City, Al Zahia and the central districts. Programme menus change between academic years and the authoritative list is the regulator's, so confirm what a school currently offers with the school itself or the Sharjah Private Education Authority rather than relying on a tutoring page. Because our lessons are delivered online, the school your child attends determines the syllabus we teach to but not whether a specialist in it is available to you.

faqs.question: What happens to the weekly slot during mock exam fortnight?
faqs.answer: We usually reduce it to nothing or one session. During mocks the student is already sitting full papers under timed conditions, which is the most valuable thing they could be doing, and adding sessions that week tends to cost sleep rather than add marks. The useful hours sit either side: one before to practise paper discipline, and one after to work through the returned script. Marking a student's own mock paper with them is worth more than any amount of topic revision, because it shows exactly where the marks left.

faqs.question: Can a tutor work to my child's school deadlines rather than a syllabus plan?
faqs.answer: That is how we prefer to run it. For Diploma students in particular, the deadlines that matter are the internal ones your child's school sets for Internal Assessments, the Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge, not the board's published windows. We take that deadline list from the student's own documents in the first session and build the term backwards from it. In a deadline week the hour becomes supervision on the student's own draft rather than new teaching, which is a different use of the same slot.

faqs.question: Do weekend morning sessions work better than weekday evenings in Sharjah?
faqs.answer: For some students, clearly yes. A primary or lower-MYP child at 19:00 after a long bus journey will not absorb a new method however well it is taught, and that is a scheduling fact rather than a motivation problem. Weekend mornings have no school run, no activity and no sibling pick-up competing with them, so longer sessions become viable at an age where they would not be midweek. They are also the first slots to be claimed each term, so ask early if that is what you want.

faqs.question: Which mandatory UAE subjects sit on top of an IGCSE timetable?
faqs.answer: Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies. UAE private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond those, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations, which is why they appear alongside the board's subjects. Dubai's regulator publishes the clearest mechanics: instructional time calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, a minimum of about 25 minutes advised per lesson, and separate classes required for Arab and non-Arab students. First-language and additional-language Arabic are different courses, so the tutor must match the stream your child actually sits.

faqs.question: How many hours a week does a DP2 student in Sharjah realistically have spare?
faqs.answer: Fewer than parents assume, and the hours are unevenly distributed. Across an ordinary teaching week a DP2 student has perhaps two or three hours that are genuinely free rather than already committed to their own coursework and reading. In a deadline fortnight they have close to none. That is why one well-placed 90-minute session usually beats three hopeful hours, and why the content of the slot has to change between teaching and supervision depending on what the student is carrying that week.

faqs.question: Is it worth starting tutoring in November for a May exam?
faqs.answer: Yes, and November is close to the ideal moment for a May series. There is still time to change technique rather than only revise, the student has returned work from the autumn term to diagnose from, and the intensive phase has not started so the sessions are cheaper and more available. Starting in March limits the honest offer to revision support. Starting after the entry deadline also means the tier your child is sitting is fixed, so for Cambridge candidates the November entry window is worth watching for reasons beyond tutoring.

faqs.question: What do we do if my son has football training on the only free evening?
faqs.answer: Move the session rather than the training. A weekend morning slot, or a later start on a different weekday, almost always works better than cancelling a commitment a teenager cares about, and a resentful student in an hour they did not want is poor value at any rate. Because lessons are online and no tutor is routing a car around your address, a slot can sit at an unusual time without a premium. Tell us the fixed commitments first and we build the week around them.

faqs.question: How do you handle a lesson when the internet drops mid-session?
faqs.answer: The shared board and the annotated work are saved as the session runs, so nothing written is lost when a connection fails. In practice short drops are handled by reconnecting and picking up from the board; a longer outage means the remainder of the session is rescheduled rather than counted. Students keep access to the saved board afterwards, which is one practical advantage over a session in a room, where the only record is whatever the student managed to copy into their own book at the time.

sharjah/al-suyoh.closingHeading: Tell us when your child is actually free
sharjah/al-suyoh.closingBody: Start with the real return time, the board and level your child sits, and two recent pieces of marked work. From those three things we can tell you what session length the job needs, which evening or weekend morning it should sit in, and how the plan should change through mocks, Ramadan, the final phase and study leave. The introductory session is at no charge, one per family, with the student present, so you can test the match before committing to anything. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video, which is why the time you choose is the time it happens.

intro.heading: Who lives in Al Taawun, and what their report cards look like
paragraphs: Al Taawun is a line of residential towers running north from the Khalid Lagoon towards the Dubai boundary at Al Mamzar, dense, almost entirely apartment-based and more mixed in first language than any other part of central Sharjah. Arabic-speaking households from across the region live in the same buildings as South Asian, Egyptian, Sudanese and Filipino families. That mix is the single most useful fact about tutoring here, because it determines which of two parallel timetables a child is struggling with.

Every child in a UAE private school carries both. The federal position is that private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. So a Year 10 pupil in Al Taawun sits Cambridge or Pearson subjects and, in the same week, Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies lessons that are not part of the international specification at all and are graded separately.

What happens in practice is that the mandatory grades are the ones nobody plans for. A family will arrive asking for help in chemistry while the Arabic grade on the same report is two bands lower, because Arabic has been treated as a given rather than as a subject with technique, vocabulary load and assessment criteria of its own. Among non-Arab households, Arabic as an additional language is very often the lowest grade on an otherwise respectable report.

Among Arabic-speaking households the pattern inverts. The child is fluent at home, performs well in Arabic as a first language, and struggles with the extended academic English that Cambridge science papers and Diploma essays demand. Both families need tutoring. They need completely different tutoring, and a provider that treats them as the same enquiry will mis-serve one of them.

There is a timing dimension too, and it is particular to this stream. Language work rewards short frequent contact, while a Higher Level science problem needs a long uninterrupted run. In a neighbourhood where the usable evening is roughly 6:30pm to 9pm, those two demands compete for the same hours, and the family that stacks both onto one evening ends up doing neither properly. Splitting them across the week is the whole of the scheduling advice for a two-stream household.

IB Gram delivers all of it one-to-one over live video. IB Gram does not visit homes in the UAE, and in-home tutoring is a service run only in India. For Al Taawun specifically the advantage is streaming: an Arabic first-language specialist and a Pearson 4CH1 chemistry specialist are two different people, and video delivery means a family can have both in the same week without either of them driving through Al Taawun Street at seven in the evening.

sharjah/al-taawun.programmesIntro: Four strands of study matter to an Al Taawun family, and the fourth is the one almost no tutoring page describes. Each entry below says what the strand assesses and what it means for a household in this part of Sharjah.

programmes.name: Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies
programmes.description: Three subject areas every private school in the UAE teaches regardless of which international curriculum it is licensed for. They are graded separately, carry their own assessment expectations, and in Dubai the published guidance sets instructional time using a 40-minute lesson unit, with schools permitted to vary lesson length provided the total weekly time is met and with at least 25 minutes advised for any mandatory lesson.

Sharjah schools answer to the Sharjah Private Education Authority, which approves curricula, programmes, courses and assessment methods in the emirate, so an Al Taawun parent should confirm the exact stream and timetable with their own school rather than assume the Dubai document applies unchanged.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Eight to ten subjects examined at the end of Year 11 by syllabus or specification code, with tiering in Cambridge sciences and maths that fixes the attainable grade. Marks turn on command terms as much as on content, which is why bilingual candidates who understand the material can still underperform on a six-mark question.
programmes.countryNote: In a neighbourhood with this many second-language English speakers, the highest-return intervention at IGCSE is usually not more content. It is teaching the child to decode what a question verb is asking for, and to write an answer that names the process, states the direction and links the consequence. That is a teachable skill with a short payback period.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects across two years, three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Language acquisition sits in group two, and candidates may take Arabic at ab initio, Standard Level or Higher Level depending on their background, which is a decision with real consequences for the points total.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma candidates from Arabic-speaking Al Taawun households often have a genuine strategic advantage available to them in group two that families overlook, and a corresponding risk in group one if English is the weaker academic language. Working that out in year one, with the school's coordinator, is worth more than any amount of catch-up tutoring in year two.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups marked against four criteria, each scored 1 to 8 and converted by the school into a 1 to 7 grade. Language acquisition runs in phases rather than year groups, so a child can sit in a phase that no longer matches their ability in either direction.
programmes.countryNote: Phase placement in Arabic is the recurring Al Taawun question in the Middle Years Programme. A child placed in an early phase because they joined the school with no Arabic may be held there long after they have outgrown it, and the report looks fine while progress has stalled. Ask the school which phase the child is in and what moving up would require.

sharjah/al-taawun.subjectsIntro: The subject list below reflects what Al Taawun households actually request, which is a mix of the mandatory stream and the academic stream. Each entry names where marks are lost rather than what the subject contains.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first language
subjects.description: Fluent speakers lose marks on formal register, dictation accuracy and structured literary response rather than on comprehension. Standard Arabic rather than dialect is what is assessed, and the gap between the two is the work.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Script fluency, verb patterns and listening remain the three bottlenecks for non-Arab pupils. Progress comes from short frequent practice with reading aloud, which suits two forty-minute sessions a week far better than one long one.

subjects.name: Islamic Education
subjects.description: Taught and assessed differently for the two groups, including in the language of instruction. Pupils lose marks on memorisation accuracy and on structured written answers rather than on understanding of the material.

subjects.name: Social and moral studies
subjects.description: Content is set centrally and schools may not substitute material without prior ministry permission, so tutoring works to the prescribed content. Written answers need specific examples from that content rather than general reasoning.

subjects.name: English as a second language and English A
subjects.description: Summary and reading-for-detail questions reward precision over fluency at IGCSE. At Diploma level the individual oral and guided analysis need a claim about how a text works, which second-language candidates can build quickly once shown the structure.

subjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580
subjects.description: Extended candidates meet functions, transformations and histogram density that Core candidates never see. Language is rarely the barrier here, which is why maths is often the first subject to improve for bilingual pupils.

subjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620
subjects.description: Mole calculations, electrolysis and the qualitative analysis tables carry the Extended difficulty. Precise terminology about ions and half-equations earns more than additional content coverage.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Fields and circular motion require algebra and physical reasoning to run together. Paper 1 tests whether a candidate can recognise which relationship applies before calculating anything.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: A long syllabus where marks are lost to imprecise language. Examiners want the structure named, the mechanism linked and the direction stated, and that discipline is teachable independently of content.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Application to the stimulus organisation earns the marks, not reproduction of a tool. Candidates who list both sides without reaching a defended judgement stall in the middle of the range.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: Worth up to three points together and capable of ending a diploma if a submission is flagged. Support is question framing, criteria explanation and feedback on the student's own drafts, never supplied text.

sections.heading: Four Al Taawun households, four different first problems
paragraphs: Tutoring enquiries from this neighbourhood sort into four groups, and the mistake families make is reading advice written for a different group. A plan that works for an Arabic-speaking Diploma candidate will not work for a non-Arab Year 9 pupil who has just been moved up a phase in Arabic.

The first group is Arabic-speaking households with strong mandatory-subject grades and weaker academic English. Their work is extended academic writing: structuring an argument, decoding a question verb, and writing a science answer that names a mechanism rather than describing an outcome. The second group is non-Arab households where the international subjects are fine and Arabic as an additional language is dragging the report down. That is a vocabulary, script and listening problem, and it needs frequency.

The third group is bilingual households where the child is fluent in conversation in both languages and formally assessed in neither at the level the report implies. These are the hardest to diagnose, because the child sounds capable in a trial lesson. The fourth is the mid-year arrival placed into a stream by year group rather than by prior attainment, who may be sitting in an Arabic class two phases away from their actual level in either direction.

Sorting yourself into one of these groups takes about ten minutes with the last school report and costs nothing. Look at the mandatory-subject rows rather than skipping to the sciences, compare the grade with the comment, and note whether the weak grades cluster in language or in written structure across every subject. A report where English, biology and history all slipped together is telling you something different from a report where only Arabic is low.

sections.heading: The subjects that sit beside the international curriculum
paragraphs: This is the gap in every competing page in this market. Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies appear on tutoring sites as a chip in a subject list, never as a stream with rules, streams and assessment expectations of its own. For a household in Al Taawun they are half the report card.

The federal baseline is that private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. Dubai's regulator has published the most detailed public account of what that means in practice, and it is worth reading even if your child is at a Sharjah school, because it shows the shape of the requirement: mandatory in all private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, with implementation required by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, or April 2026 for schools whose year starts in April.

The same guidance sets out how the subjects must be organised. Schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and social studies, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, Arabic is the primary language for social studies for Arab students, and the school's licensed-curriculum language applies for non-Arabs in Islamic Education and in moral, social and cultural studies.

Two further details matter to anyone buying tutoring in this stream. Instructional time is calculated using a 40-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided the total weekly time is met, and at least 25 minutes is advised for any mandatory subject lesson. And the use of any different or additional content, without prior permission from the Ministry of Education, is strictly prohibited, which means a tutor in this stream works to the prescribed content rather than importing material from elsewhere.

sections.heading: Choosing an Arabic route in the Diploma, and what it costs to get wrong
paragraphs: For a Diploma candidate in Al Taawun, group two is a strategic decision rather than an administrative one, and it is usually made in a hurry at the end of the Middle Years Programme. The options differ in what they assume about prior exposure, and a candidate placed too high loses points while a candidate placed too low may be refused entry to the course by the school.

The broad shape is this. Ab initio is designed for candidates with no meaningful prior study of the language and is available at Standard Level only. Language B sits above it for candidates with some years of study, at Standard or Higher Level. Language A is for candidates studying the language as a literature or language-and-literature course rather than as an acquisition subject, which for a fluent Arabic speaker may be the right place to be and for a conversational speaker usually is not.

The trap for a bilingual household is assuming that speaking Arabic at home qualifies a candidate for Language A. Conversational fluency and the formal literary analysis a Language A course demands are different competencies, and the gap between them has cost many capable candidates points they expected to bank. The reverse trap, for a non-Arab candidate who has studied Arabic in school since Year 3, is being parked in ab initio where the course offers nothing new.

The decision belongs to the student, the parent and the school's coordinator together, with evidence rather than assumption. What a tutor can usefully do beforehand is assess formal written Arabic against the demands of each route and say plainly which is the honest fit. Confirm every course option and level against the school's own subject offer, because not all schools run all routes.

sections.heading: What the academic stream needs at the same time
paragraphs: A family dealing with two timetables has to decide which one gets the attention, and the answer depends on the year group rather than on which grade looks worse.

Below Year 9, the language stream usually deserves priority. Arabic is cumulative, a gap compounds, and the years before the public examination course begins are the cheap years in which to close it. Academic subjects at that stage are still broad enough that a weak term does not have lasting consequences.

From Year 10 the balance shifts, because the international subjects are now attached to an examination with an entry deadline and a grade that follows the child to university. The mandatory subjects still matter for the report and for progression within the school, but the triage order changes: the examined course comes first, with language work kept running at low intensity rather than dropped entirely.

In the Diploma, both are examined and both count, so the question becomes which subject has the most recoverable marks per hour spent. That is usually a subject where the candidate understands the content and loses marks on structure, because structure is teachable in weeks while missing content takes months. A tutor who cannot tell you which of those two problems your child has is not yet in a position to plan.

There is one argument for keeping a low-intensity language session running even in an examination year, and it is practical rather than sentimental. Dropping Arabic entirely for a year means returning to it from further behind, and in a household where the mandatory grades affect progression within the school, a term of silence can create a problem that outlasts the exam it was meant to help. One short session a fortnight holds ground cheaply.

sections.heading: What each stream costs in AED around Al Taawun
paragraphs: Nobody in this market publishes rates, so the bands below are set out plainly as market figures read in October 2026, with the kind of provider that charges each. They are not an IB Gram price list; IB Gram quotes after a consultation because the figure depends on subject, level and how many weeks remain.

Language-stream tutoring generally sits at the lower end of the academic range, because the tutor pool is larger in a country where Arabic is widely spoken and because sessions are shorter. Specialist Diploma Higher Level work sits at the top. In-home visiting rates in the UAE run from AED 180 to 350 in Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 rate table, with independent home tutors asking up to AED 500, and those figures absorb travel as well as teaching.

The arithmetic that matters for a two-stream household is weekly rather than hourly. Two forty-minute language sessions plus one sixty-minute academic session is a realistic Al Taawun pattern, and costing it per week rather than per hour usually produces a different decision about frequency than a rate card does.

Ask what the figure includes: marked work, a written note, continuity of tutor across terms, and the policy when a session is missed. A rate without those answers is not comparable with one that has them.

One further caution about published figures in this market. Three of the main providers researched in October 2026 publish no price at all, and two of those that do quote in dollars, a currency no Sharjah family transacts in. A rate quoted without a currency, a date and a session length is not information. sections.heading: The home-tutor search, answered for Al Taawun
paragraphs: Families here search for a home tutor because that is the established phrase, and in a neighbourhood this dense it is also a realistic option: a tutor can walk between towers. For primary homework support and for conversational Arabic practice, a local visiting tutor is a perfectly sensible choice and always has been.

The model runs into two walls. The first is specialism: the number of people within walking distance who can teach Diploma Higher Level chemistry, or who know how Pearson assesses practical skills differently from Cambridge, is small. The second is the stream rule. A child in the non-Arab Islamic Education stream is taught in the school's licensed-curriculum language, and a tutor who teaches the Arab-stream content in Standard Arabic is teaching the wrong course competently.

IB Gram does not visit homes in the UAE, and in-home tutoring is offered only in India. Al Taawun families are taught one-to-one over live video, which is what makes it possible to put a first-language Arabic specialist and a board-specific science specialist in the same week. The comparison below is the one to make before paying for either model.

The limits are worth stating. A video session needs a quiet room, which in a shared apartment takes arranging, and younger children need an adult nearby at first. Reading aloud works well on video; laboratory bench time does not exist on video and belongs to the school.

A note on handwriting, which matters more in the language stream than anywhere else. Arabic script is produced with a pen, and a child whose written letter forms are the problem needs the tutor to see the page rather than a typed answer. A phone propped above a notebook, or a cheap graphics tablet, solves this completely and is worth arranging before the first session rather than discovering in week three.

sections.heading: Who regulates what, and what nobody can claim
paragraphs: Sharjah private schools answer to the Sharjah Private Education Authority, which the federal portal describes as regulating private education in the emirate, and whose remit includes approving tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. Dubai schools answer to the Knowledge and Human Development Authority. Abu Dhabi and Al Ain sit with the Department of Education and Knowledge, Ras Al Khaimah with its own Department of Knowledge, and Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah with the federal Ministry of Education.

That map matters in Al Taawun because the neighbourhood straddles a boundary in practice if not on paper. A child at a Sharjah school and a neighbour at a Dubai school are subject to two different authorities on stream organisation, inspection and fees, and the two sets of published guidance are not identical in detail.

Tutors are regulated by neither. Private tuition is permitted through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, granted free of charge for two years, open to registered teachers, government and private sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Tutoring without the permit attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule has been published.

One sentence needs saying plainly. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from SPEA, the Dubai authority, the Department of Education and Knowledge, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, and claims none. Schools are required to ensure their own Arabic and Islamic Education teachers hold the appropriate authorisation from their regulator; that is a requirement on schools, and no tutoring platform inherits it.

sections.heading: Running two timetables without losing the week
paragraphs: The practical question for an Al Taawun family is how to add tutoring to a week that already contains two sets of homework. The sequence below is what works rather than what sounds thorough.

Start by establishing the stream. Ask the school, in writing, which Arabic stream and which Islamic Education stream the child sits in, what the language of instruction is for each, and when placement is reviewed. That single answer determines which tutor is appropriate and prevents the most common mismatch in this neighbourhood.

Then bring the academic detail: board, syllabus or specification code, tier and level, plus the most recent report with the mandatory-subject grades included rather than cropped out. Agree the slots next, keeping the language sessions short and early in the week and the academic session later, and never stack two sessions on one evening for a child below Year 10.

Run a short diagnostic block in each stream before committing to a term, and ask for the plan in writing. Then set one review point against the next school report rather than two separate ones, because a household running two streams needs a single moment to judge both and adjust. If a specialist is unavailable in a scarce subject or stream at your hour, expect to be told so directly.

Expect to drop something. A week that already holds two sets of homework cannot absorb three tutoring sessions without something else going, and the honest version of this conversation names what that will be before the first lesson rather than after a month of strain. Most Al Taawun families land on two sessions a week in term time, rising to three only in the final weeks before a series, and that is a sustainable shape rather than a compromise.

faqs.question: Does my child have to take Arabic if they are at an international school in Al Taawun?
faqs.answer: Yes. The federal position is that private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. That applies regardless of whether the school is licensed for a British, American or International Baccalaureate curriculum. The stream your child sits in, and the language of instruction for it, depends on whether the pupil is classified as Arab or non-Arab under the published rules. Your school can confirm the stream and when placement is reviewed.

faqs.question: Why are Arab and non-Arab pupils taught these subjects in separate classes?
faqs.answer: Because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. The published Dubai guidance states that for Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and social studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, and that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited. Standard Arabic is the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, while non-Arabs are taught Islamic Education and moral, social and cultural studies in the school's licensed-curriculum language. A tutor has to teach to the correct stream.

faqs.question: My non-Arab child has the lowest grade in Arabic. Is that fixable before the end of the year?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, and faster than families expect, because the barrier is rarely intelligence. It is script fluency, verb patterns and listening, all of which respond to frequency. Two sessions of about forty minutes a week with reading aloud and immediate correction does more than one ninety-minute session. The published guidance calculates mandatory-subject time in 40-minute units and advises at least 25 minutes for any such lesson, which is a reasonable indication of the right working unit for tutoring as well.

faqs.question: Which Arabic route should a Diploma candidate from an Arabic-speaking household take?
faqs.answer: That depends on formal written Arabic rather than on spoken fluency, and it should be settled with the school's Diploma coordinator. Broadly, ab initio is for candidates with little prior study and is Standard Level only, Language B is for candidates with several years of study at either level, and Language A is a literature or language-and-literature course. Speaking Arabic at home does not by itself qualify a candidate for Language A, and that misplacement has cost many students points. Assess the written work before choosing.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover both Arabic and my child's science subjects?
faqs.answer: Rarely well. Arabic as a first language and Diploma Higher Level chemistry are different trainings, and a tutor who claims both tends to be strong in one. The arrangement that works in Al Taawun is two specialists in the same week: short frequent language sessions earlier, the academic session later, and nothing stacked on the same evening for a child below Year 10. Because lessons are delivered over video, having two tutors costs nothing in travel or logistics.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a tutor to a tower in Al Taawun?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not make home visits anywhere in the UAE, and in-home tutoring is a service offered only in India. Al Taawun families are taught one-to-one over live video with a shared whiteboard and screen sharing. In this neighbourhood the practical gain is stream matching: the choice of Arabic specialist is not limited to whoever is walking distance away, and the academic specialist is chosen by syllabus code rather than by postcode.

faqs.question: What do these subjects cost compared with a science or maths tutor?
faqs.answer: Market rates read in October 2026 put qualified online subject tutors at AED 150 to 300 an hour, which is where most Arabic and Islamic Education tutoring sits, and IB or IGCSE specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above. In-home visiting rates run AED 180 to 500 because they absorb travel, per Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table and independent home tutors. For a two-stream household the useful number is the weekly total rather than the hourly rate. IB Gram quotes after a consultation.

faqs.question: Can a tutor use their own Arabic or Islamic Education materials?
faqs.answer: Within limits. The published guidance states that for the mandatory subjects, the use of any different or additional content, without prior permission from the Ministry of Education, is strictly prohibited. In practice a tutor works to the content the school is teaching, using their own practice questions and explanations rather than a different syllabus. Ask a prospective tutor which textbook and unit sequence your school uses; if they cannot answer, they are planning to teach a course your child is not sitting.

faqs.question: My child was placed in an Arabic phase on arrival and has never been moved. Is that normal?
faqs.answer: It is common and it is worth challenging. Phase or stream placement is often decided at enrolment on the basis of no prior Arabic, and then carried forward unexamined while the child outgrows it. The report can look satisfactory the whole time, because the child is being assessed against the expectations of the phase they sit in. Ask the school how placement was decided, when it is reviewed, and what evidence would support a move. A tutor can assess the written and spoken level independently.

faqs.question: Does Arabic count towards the five subjects the Ministry requires for equivalency?
faqs.answer: No. The published guidance reported in July 2026 states that Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects for the GCSE or IGCSE count, which asks for five accredited subjects at no lower than grade E or grade 3, plus one A-Level at grade E or two AS-Levels at the same grade. That does not make either subject optional at school, since both are required in UAE private schools regardless of curriculum. Verify the current rule on moe.gov.ae before relying on it.

faqs.question: Which stream should take priority if we can only afford one tutor?
faqs.answer: Below Year 9, the language stream, because Arabic is cumulative and a gap compounds while a weak term in a broad academic subject rarely has lasting consequences. From Year 10, the examined international subject, because it is attached to an entry deadline and a grade that follows the child onward, with language work kept running at low intensity rather than dropped. In the Diploma, choose the subject where the most marks are recoverable per hour, which is usually one with a structure problem rather than a content gap.

faqs.question: Is a private tutor in Sharjah required to hold a permit?
faqs.answer: Yes. Private tutoring is regulated by permit through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. The permit is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Anyone tutoring without it is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule has been published, so any specific amount quoted to you is unverified.

faqs.question: Is IB Gram approved by SPEA or by the Ministry of Education?
faqs.answer: No, and no tutoring provider should tell you it is unless it can show the permit number. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from the Sharjah Private Education Authority, the Dubai authority, the Abu Dhabi authority, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson. An operation running premises and staff requires an educational services permit from the relevant authority, which is a specific document issued to training institutes. A page claiming regulator endorsement is describing something you can check and will not find.

faqs.question: How do sessions work during Ramadan for a Sharjah family?
faqs.answer: School days shorten and the evening rhythm changes, so a 7pm slot that worked in February stops working. Most Al Taawun families move lessons to after Iftar or into the early afternoon while school hours are reduced. Language sessions in particular often work better in the shortened afternoon, when a child is less tired than late in the evening. Because lessons are over video there is no travel to renegotiate. Agree the Ramadan pattern a fortnight ahead rather than in the first week.

faqs.question: What can a tutor do on an Internal Assessment, and what must they refuse?
faqs.answer: A tutor can teach the content, interrogate a research question until it is answerable with available data, explain what each assessment criterion asks for, respond to a draft the student has written, and teach referencing and data presentation. A tutor must refuse to supply text, data, analysis or conclusions that end up in the submission. The test a parent can apply is whether the school would be comfortable seeing the tutor's contribution on the page. Anyone offering a finished assessment for a fee is selling a malpractice finding.

sharjah/al-taawun.closingHeading: Establish the stream, then build the week
sharjah/al-taawun.closingBody: An Al Taawun household is managing two timetables, and the tutoring decision that matters most is which stream the child actually sits in. Ask the school for the Arabic and Islamic Education stream in writing, send the board and syllabus code for the academic subjects, and the week can be built properly: short language sessions early, the academic session later, one review point against the next report. Lessons run one-to-one over live video, every AED band here is a market figure with its month, and the student writes every word of their own assessed work.

sharjah/al-zahia.tutorsIntro: The tutors below cover the stages Al Zahia families actually ask about: primary literacy and number, Middle Years subject support read against the criteria, and the first year of an examined course for the older siblings in the same households.

intro.heading: A young community asks earlier questions
paragraphs: Al Zahia is a planned villa and townhouse community in the inland belt of Sharjah, built in phases and occupied mostly by families with young children. Walk through it on a weekday afternoon and the age profile is obvious. There are far more eight-year-olds than seventeen-year-olds, and the tutoring enquiries follow that distribution exactly.

This changes what a useful page has to say. In the coastal districts the question is which examination technique is losing marks. Here it is more often whether a primary report that looks positive is actually describing progress, or what it means that a Middle Years pupil is scoring a 5 in science when the same pupil scored a 7 last year in a different criterion.

Criterion-marked reporting is the specific source of confusion, and it is nobody's fault. Primary programmes report against learning outcomes and portfolios rather than marks. The Middle Years Programme assesses every subject group against four criteria, each scored from 1 to 8, with the school converting the total into a 1 to 7 grade. A parent who grew up with percentages has no intuition for what a 5 in criterion C means, and the written comments rarely supply one.

The second feature of a young community is that the stakes feel low and the leverage is high. Nothing in Year 4 appears on a certificate. But reading fluency, number fluency and the habit of explaining reasoning in writing are precisely the things that compound, and a gap closed in two terms at age nine takes four times the work at age fourteen. The cheapest intervention available to any family is an early one, and it is the one least often bought.

The third is scheduling. Al Zahia children mostly attend schools in the adjacent Muwaileh belt, which is a short drive, so they are home earlier than children from the coast. That makes a genuinely useful 5pm or 5:30pm slot possible here, which matters because a nine-year-old at 7:30pm is not available for learning in any meaningful sense.

A word about the opposite risk, because it is real in a community like this one. Households here tend to be ambitious and well resourced, and the failure mode is not neglect but a nine-year-old with four activities, two tutors and no unstructured time left in the week. Early intervention earns its place only while it stays small. One measured target, a short block and a review beats intensity across five subjects at this age, every time.

IB Gram teaches one-to-one over live video. IB Gram does not visit homes in the UAE, and in-home tutoring is a service run only in India. For younger children that arrangement needs setting up properly, with a quiet room, a device with a camera and an adult nearby for the first few sessions, and it works well once those three things are in place.

sharjah/al-zahia.programmesIntro: Three programmes matter in a community this young, and the third is included because the older siblings are already in it. Each entry below says what is actually assessed, because that is what a report is reporting on.

programmes.name: IB Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: An inquiry-led framework organised around transdisciplinary themes rather than separate subjects, with assessment through portfolios, teacher observation and a final-year exhibition. There are no examinations and usually no numerical marks, so progress is reported as descriptions of what a child can do.
programmes.countryNote: The practical difficulty for an Al Zahia parent is that a warm Primary Years report is compatible with a reading age a year behind, because the report describes engagement and inquiry rather than fluency. Ask the school directly for reading age, number fluency and spelling data, and ask how it compares with where the child was six months ago.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups, each assessed against four published criteria scored from 1 to 8, giving a criterion total out of 32 that the school converts into a 1 to 7 grade using the programme's published boundaries. Tasks are completed over days with access to resources rather than under examination conditions.
programmes.countryNote: The criteria are the whole of the information. A pupil with a 7 in knowing and understanding and a 3 in communicating has a specific, fixable problem, and the single converted grade hides it completely. Ask for the criterion breakdown rather than the grade, and confirm the current criterion names and boundaries with the school.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: The examined course the older children in these households are sitting, assessed by syllabus or specification code with tiering in Cambridge maths and sciences. The move into it from a criterion-marked programme is a change in what is being measured rather than only a change in difficulty.
programmes.countryNote: For a family whose eldest is in Year 10 and whose youngest is in Year 3, it is worth noticing that the two children need opposite things. The older one needs timed papers and technique; the younger one needs fluency and confidence. Buying the same kind of tutoring for both is the usual error.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects across two years with internally assessed components, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Included here because it is the destination of the Middle Years ladder and because the skills it assumes are built long before it starts.
programmes.countryNote: The Diploma rewards sustained independent written work under deadline, which is the one thing a criterion-marked middle school rarely requires. Families who build that habit in Years 8 and 9, in small and unglamorous ways, find the Diploma transition far less dramatic than those who wait for it to become urgent.

sharjah/al-zahia.subjectsIntro: The subjects below are the ones Al Zahia households ask about most, weighted towards the younger end. Each entry names what actually goes wrong at that stage rather than listing content.

subjects.name: Primary English and reading
subjects.description: Decoding, fluency and comprehension are three separate skills, and a child can look competent in one while failing another. Fluency below age expectation is the single most predictive weakness in primary and the most responsive to short daily practice.

subjects.name: Primary mathematics
subjects.description: Number fact fluency is the bottleneck. A pupil who computes seven times eight slowly uses working memory on arithmetic that should be spent on the actual problem, which is why multi-step questions collapse while single-step ones look fine.

subjects.name: MYP Mathematics
subjects.description: Assessed on knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. Most pupils score well on the first and poorly on the third, because explaining a method is a skill nobody practises.

subjects.name: MYP Sciences
subjects.description: Assessed on knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. The design and evaluation criteria are where marks sit for most pupils, and both are about method rather than content.

subjects.name: MYP Language and literature
subjects.description: Assessed on analysing, organizing, producing text, and using language. A fluent reader can score poorly on organizing simply because nobody has taught them how to plan a response, which is a fast repair.

subjects.name: MYP Language acquisition
subjects.description: Assessed through comprehension of spoken and written text, communicating, and using language. Phase placement rather than age determines what is expected, so a report must be read against the phase the pupil sits in.

subjects.name: MYP Individuals and societies
subjects.description: Assessed on knowing and understanding, investigating, communicating, and thinking critically. Pupils lose marks for description where judgement was asked for, which is the same habit that later costs them IGCSE evaluation marks.

subjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580
subjects.description: The older sibling's subject in many of these households. Extended candidates meet functions, transformations and histogram density, and the tier is fixed at the entry deadline months before the papers are sat.

subjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610
subjects.description: A long syllabus where marks go to precise language rather than to more content. Examiners want the structure named, the mechanism linked and the direction stated, which is a writing discipline built earlier than Year 10.

subjects.name: English as a second language
subjects.description: Common in this community because many households speak another language at home. The gap is usually academic register rather than conversation, and it is most cheaply closed before an examination course begins.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Mandatory alongside the licensed curriculum in UAE private schools. Script fluency and verb patterns respond to short frequent practice, and primary is by far the cheapest stage at which to build them.

sections.heading: What a criterion-marked report is actually telling you
paragraphs: This is the most useful thing a page can give a parent in this community, and almost no competing page attempts it. The Middle Years Programme assesses every subject group against four criteria, each scored from 1 to 8, producing a total out of 32 that the school converts into a 1 to 7 grade using the programme's published boundaries. The converted grade is what parents look at, and it is the least informative number on the page.

Consider two pupils with the same converted grade in science. The first scores highly on knowing and understanding and poorly on inquiring and designing: they know the content and cannot plan an investigation. The second is the reverse: a capable experimenter who has not learned the material. Those two children need opposite interventions, and the single grade says nothing about which is which.

The criteria differ by subject group, and knowing the names makes a report legible. Mathematics is assessed on knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. Sciences on knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. Language and literature on analysing, organizing, producing text, and using language. Individuals and societies on knowing and understanding, investigating, communicating, and thinking critically.

So the request to make of the school is specific: not how is my child doing, but what were the criterion scores and which criterion has been lowest for the last two reporting cycles. That question is answerable, and its answer is a plan. Confirm the current criterion names and boundary tables with the school, since the IB revises its guides.

sections.heading: The ladder from inquiry to examination
paragraphs: Families in Al Zahia are usually at the start of a ten-year sequence, and it helps to see the whole thing once. What changes between stages is not only difficulty but the thing being measured, and each transition catches out the children who were comfortable at the stage before.

The Primary Years Programme measures inquiry, participation and the ability to make connections, reported through portfolios and observation. The Middle Years Programme measures performance against four published criteria per subject group on tasks completed over days. An examined course measures what a candidate can produce alone, under time pressure, with nothing in front of them. Those are three different skills, and a child can be excellent at the first two and untrained in the third.

The predictable consequence is a grade drop at each transition that reflects an untrained skill rather than a fall in ability. It is most visible between the Middle Years Programme and the Diploma, and it is why so many families in neighbouring districts contact a tutor in the first term of Diploma year one. Al Zahia has the opportunity to pre-empt that, because its children are still years away from it.

The practical version is undramatic. From Year 8, twenty minutes of timed writing in each session, a mark scheme read as a set of instructions, and one longer planned piece a month. No pressure, no examination language, just the habit. Families who do this report that the eventual transition is uneventful, which is precisely the outcome worth buying.

sections.heading: Primary signals worth acting on, and ones that are noise
paragraphs: Parents of young children are given a great deal of advice about what to worry about and very little about what to ignore. In a community with this many primary-age children, that distinction is the most useful thing on this page.

The signals worth acting on share a feature: they are measurable and they compound. Reading fluency below age expectation compounds, because every subject is read. Slow recall of number facts compounds, because it consumes the working memory a multi-step problem needs. Avoidance of writing compounds, because the gap between what a child can think and what they can put on paper widens with every year it is left.

The signals that are usually noise also share a feature: they are developmental and they resolve. Untidy handwriting at seven, reluctance to read aloud in a group, being slower than a precocious classmate, disliking a particular teacher's subject for a term. None of these predict much, and tutoring bought in response to them teaches a child that there is something wrong with them when there is not.

The test that separates the two is simple and costs nothing: ask the school for data rather than impressions. Reading age, a fluency measure, a spelling age, a number fact check. Numbers that are behind and not moving are worth acting on. Numbers that are behind and improving are usually fine. Comments without numbers are not a diagnosis, however warmly they are written.

There is one signal that belongs in neither column and deserves its own response: a child who used to be fine and is now not. A drop on a measure that was previously on track is worth asking about directly, because it is more often a change in circumstances, eyesight, hearing, sleep or something social than a change in ability. Rule those out before buying any tutoring at all.

sections.heading: The two things that genuinely compound
paragraphs: If a family in this community does only one thing before secondary school, it should be to make reading and number recall automatic. Everything else in education is built on those two, and both are cheap to fix early and expensive to fix late.

Reading fluency is not comprehension and should not be confused with it. A child who decodes accurately but slowly spends so much attention on the mechanics that little is left for meaning, which looks like a comprehension problem and is not. The remedy is volume of reading at the right level with some of it aloud, in short daily sessions, and it is measurable: fluency measures move within weeks when the practice is consistent.

Number fact automaticity works the same way. A pupil who has to compute a multiplication rather than recall it is using working memory on arithmetic, so a two-step problem fails even though both steps are understood. This is why able children appear to be bad at word problems. Ten focused minutes a day for six weeks changes it, and almost no school timetable has room for that.

Both of these are also unglamorous, which is why they are undersold. A tutoring provider makes more from a weekly hour on the current topic than from telling a parent to spend ten minutes a day on times tables. The honest version is that for a primary child, the second is usually worth more, and the right use of a tutor at that age is to set it up, teach the parent how to run it, and check it every few weeks.

sections.heading: Why the same money buys more at nine than at fifteen
paragraphs: This is an argument about cost, so it should use numbers. Market rates read in October 2026 put budget online tutoring at roughly AED 33 to 150 an hour, qualified online subject tutors at AED 150 to 300, and IB or IGCSE specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above. In-home visiting rates run AED 180 to 350 in Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 rate table, with independent home tutors up to AED 500 because travel is absorbed. None of these are IB Gram prices; IB Gram quotes after a consultation.

Notice the shape of that. A primary fluency problem can be addressed by a capable tutor at the lower end of the market, in thirty-minute sessions, over a term. The same underlying weakness at Year 11, now presenting as lost marks across three subjects in an examined year, needs a specialist at the top of the market, in longer sessions, under time pressure, with less chance of a complete fix.

The gap is not only price per hour. It is hours required, and the number of subjects affected, and whether the work is remedial or developmental. A child who reads fluently at nine does not need an English tutor at fifteen for that reason. A child who does not will probably need help in several subjects, because every one of them is read.

Which produces an uncomfortable conclusion for a tutoring business and a useful one for a parent. The highest-return tutoring purchase available in Al Zahia is a small, cheap, early one, and the least efficient is a large expensive late one. Spending at the right stage is a bigger lever than choosing between providers.

sections.heading: Choosing a tutor for a nine-year-old
paragraphs: The criteria for a primary tutor are almost the opposite of those for a Diploma tutor, and families applying the wrong checklist end up with a well-qualified subject specialist who cannot hold a child's attention for twenty minutes.

What matters at this age is pace, warmth and the ability to make a short session feel like a game rather than an assessment. A primary session that ends with the child wanting to come back is doing its job; one that ends with a sense of failure has cost more than it bought. Subject depth is almost irrelevant: nobody needs a chemistry postgraduate to teach number bonds.

What also matters, and is easy to check, is whether the tutor will tell you what to do between sessions. The real work at primary age happens in the ten minutes a day the family runs, and a tutor's most valuable output is a simple routine a parent can maintain plus a check on whether it is working. A tutor who sets no practice is selling an hour rather than a result.

On the practical side, a video session with a young child needs arranging rather than improvising. A quiet room, a device on a stable surface at the child's eye level, a notebook and pencil in shot, an adult nearby for the first few sessions, and a fixed early-evening time before tiredness arrives. In Al Zahia, where the school run is short, that usually means 5pm or 5:30pm rather than after dinner.
