sections.heading: Home tutoring in a villa community, honestly
paragraphs: Al Zahia is a villa community with space, which makes the in-home model more appealing here than in a tower block. A tutor arriving at a house with a study and a dining table is a straightforwardly pleasant arrangement, and for primary support there is nothing wrong with it in principle.

The constraints are supply and specialism. This is a newer inland community and the local tutor supply has not caught up with the population, so what is available is often someone travelling from Muwaileh, the coastal districts or across the Dubai boundary, charging for the journey and offering only the hours the journey allows. For a 5pm primary slot, that radius is a real limit.

IB Gram does not visit homes in the UAE, and in-home tutoring is a service offered only in India. Al Zahia families are taught one-to-one over live video. For primary work the honest comparison is that in-home has an advantage in the room and online has an advantage in choice and reliability of the hour, and for a Middle Years criterion problem or an older sibling's examined subject the choice of specialist matters considerably more.

The limits of video with young children should be stated rather than brushed past. Under about eight, an adult needs to be nearby. Handwriting work needs the page in shot, which a phone propped above a notebook solves. And a child who will not engage with a screen will not engage with a screen, which is what the first session is for finding out.

sections.heading: Starting early without over-scheduling
paragraphs: The risk in a young, ambitious community is not neglect. It is a nine-year-old with four activities and two tutors, who is tired every evening and no longer likes anything. The point of early intervention is that it can be small, and small only works if it is actually small.

Start by asking the school for data rather than opinions: reading age, fluency, spelling, number facts, and the criterion breakdown if the child is in the Middle Years Programme. That request is reasonable and most schools answer it. Then identify one thing. Not three. One measurable weakness that is behind and not moving.

Buy a short block aimed at that one thing, with a routine for the family to run between sessions and a review in six to eight weeks against the same measure. If the number has moved, stop or move to the next thing. If it has not, change the approach rather than adding hours. This is a cheap, unglamorous cycle and it is what actually works at this age.

Then protect the rest of the week. A primary child needs unstructured time more than a second tutor, and a Middle Years pupil needs sleep more than a fourth session. Families here can afford to be patient because they have years in hand, and patience plus one measured target beats intensity across five.

Keep the child out of the diagnosis conversation and in the work. A nine-year-old who hears that they are behind at reading tends to read less, and the self-image formed at that age outlasts the gap by years. The useful framing is specific and neutral: we are going to get faster at this one thing, here is how we will know, and here is when we stop. Children respond well to a finite task with a visible end.

process.title: Ask the school for data, not opinions
process.description: Reading age, fluency, spelling, number facts, and the criterion breakdown for a Middle Years pupil. Comments without numbers are not a diagnosis, and this request is both reasonable and usually answered within a week.

process.title: Pick one measurable target
process.description: One weakness that is behind and not improving, rather than three that look untidy. A single target with a number attached can be reviewed honestly in six weeks; a general wish to do better cannot be reviewed at all.

process.title: Buy small and short
process.description: Thirty to forty minutes, twice a week for primary, or one weekly session aimed at a named criterion for a Middle Years pupil. Buying a secondary-sized arrangement for a younger child wastes money and tires the child.

process.title: Run the ten minutes a day
process.description: Ask the tutor for a short routine the family maintains between sessions, because at primary age that is where the progress happens. A tutor who sets no practice between sessions is selling an hour rather than a change.

process.title: Review against the same measure
process.description: Re-check the original number after six to eight weeks. If it has moved, stop or move on; if it has not, change the approach rather than adding hours. This cycle is cheap and it is what distinguishes early intervention from early spending.

whyPoints.title: Criterion reports read properly
whyPoints.description: A converted Middle Years grade hides the information; the four criterion scores contain it. Sessions target the criterion that has been lowest across two reporting cycles rather than the subject as a whole, which is usually a method problem rather than a content one.

whyPoints.title: Session length matched to age
whyPoints.description: Thirty to forty minutes twice a week for primary, a single focused hour for Middle Years, longer only where the work genuinely needs it. A tired nine-year-old in a ninety-minute session is being supervised, not taught.

whyPoints.title: Honest about what is noise
whyPoints.description: Untidy handwriting at seven and disliking a subject for a term predict very little, and tutoring bought in response teaches a child something unhelpful about themselves. Saying so costs a sale and is the right advice.

whyPoints.title: The parent gets a routine, not just a lesson
whyPoints.description: At primary age most of the progress happens in ten minutes a day at home. A session should end with a simple routine for the family to run and a check on whether the last one worked.

whyPoints.title: Delivery stated plainly
whyPoints.description: IB Gram does not visit homes anywhere in the UAE; in-home tutoring is an India-only service. Lessons are one-to-one over live video, and no regulator or examination board has approved, accredited or licensed IB Gram.

whyPoints.title: No promises about outcomes
whyPoints.description: No grade guarantee at any age, no claimed success rates, and no statistics without a source. Where a figure appears on this page it carries the kind of provider that published it and the month it was read.

faqs.question: What does a Middle Years Programme grade of 5 actually mean?
faqs.answer: Less than you would think on its own. Each subject group is assessed against four criteria, each scored from 1 to 8, giving a total out of 32 that the school converts into a 1 to 7 grade using the programme's published boundaries. Two pupils with the same 5 can have completely different profiles, one strong on knowing and understanding and weak on communicating, the other the reverse. Ask the school for the criterion scores rather than the grade, and confirm the current criterion names with them.

faqs.question: My child's primary report is warm but says nothing specific. What should I ask for?
faqs.answer: Numbers. Reading age and a fluency measure, a spelling age, and a check on number fact recall, plus how each compares with six months ago. Primary reporting describes engagement and inquiry rather than attainment, so a positive report is entirely compatible with a reading age a year behind. A measure that is behind and not moving is worth acting on; one that is behind and improving usually means the school's intervention is already working.

faqs.question: Is tutoring at primary age too early?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on what is being bought. A weekly hour of general topic coverage for a seven-year-old is usually a waste and can teach a child that there is something wrong with them. Two thirty-minute sessions a week aimed at a single measurable weakness, with a short daily routine for the family to run, is among the highest-return educational spending available. The question is not whether to start early but whether the target is specific and measurable.

faqs.question: Which Middle Years criterion is my child most likely losing marks on?
faqs.answer: In maths and sciences it is usually the applied and evaluative criteria rather than knowing and understanding: applying mathematics in real-life contexts, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating. In language and literature it is often organizing, because planning a response is rarely taught explicitly. The pattern matters because none of these are content problems, so more revision of material does nothing. Ask for two reporting cycles of criterion scores and the weakest one will usually be obvious.

faqs.question: Why do strong Middle Years students struggle in the first Diploma term?
faqs.answer: Because the thing being measured changes. Middle Years tasks are criterion-marked, completed over days with access to resources, and they reward investigation, process and reflection. The Diploma asks for timed written output with nothing in front of the candidate, across more content, plus genuinely independent assessed work. The first-term drop is usually an untrained skill rather than a fall in ability, and families in Al Zahia have years in which to pre-empt it cheaply.

faqs.question: What should a nine-year-old's session look like?
faqs.answer: Thirty to forty minutes, twice a week, early in the evening before tiredness arrives, aimed at one thing rather than at a syllabus. It should feel closer to a game than an assessment, end with the child willing to return, and finish with a short routine for the family to run during the week. Subject depth in the tutor matters far less than pace and warmth at this age: nobody needs a specialist to teach number bonds.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a tutor to a villa in Al Zahia?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not make home visits anywhere in the UAE, and in-home tutoring is a service run only in India. Al Zahia families are taught one-to-one over live video. In a villa community the in-home model is genuinely appealing, and the honest comparison is that it has an advantage in the room while online has an advantage in the choice of tutor and the reliability of the hour, which matters most for criterion work and for older siblings.

faqs.question: How do video lessons work with a young child?
faqs.answer: They work once the setup is right, and poorly if it is improvised. A young child needs a quiet room, a device on a stable surface at eye level, a notebook and pencil visible in shot, and an adult nearby for the first few sessions. Under about eight, assume an adult stays within earshot throughout. Handwriting work needs the page in view, which a phone propped above the notebook solves. The first session is the test of whether the child engages at all.

faqs.question: What time of day is best for an Al Zahia child?
faqs.answer: Earlier than in the coastal districts. Because the school run into the Muwaileh belt is short, children here are often home by mid-afternoon, which makes 5pm or 5:30pm a genuinely usable slot. That matters because a nine-year-old at 7:30pm is not available for learning in any useful sense. For older pupils the later evening is fine, and Saturday morning remains the best slot for anything long or written.

faqs.question: Should I worry about untidy handwriting in Year 2?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Motor development varies widely at that age and most of it resolves without intervention, and tutoring bought in response often teaches a child that something is wrong when nothing is. Revisit it if it is still a barrier at around nine, or sooner if the child is avoiding written work altogether, because avoidance is a different and more significant signal. The things genuinely worth acting on in primary are reading fluency and number fact recall.

faqs.question: How much does early support cost compared with fixing it later?
faqs.answer: Market rates read in October 2026 put budget online tutoring at roughly AED 33 to 150 an hour, qualified subject tutors at AED 150 to 300, and IB or IGCSE specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above. The difference is not only the rate: a fluency problem addressed in primary is one subject and a term, while the same weakness at Year 11 affects every subject that is read and needs a specialist under time pressure. Early is cheaper in rate and in hours.

faqs.question: My child reads accurately but slowly. Is that a comprehension problem?
faqs.answer: Usually not, and treating it as one wastes a term. A child who decodes accurately but slowly spends most of their attention on the mechanics, leaving little for meaning, which looks exactly like weak comprehension. The remedy is volume of reading at the right level, with some of it aloud, in short daily sessions. Fluency measures move within weeks when the practice is consistent, which is also how you confirm the diagnosis was right.

faqs.question: Does Arabic need to start in primary if it is compulsory anyway?
faqs.answer: Starting early is considerably cheaper than catching up later. Arabic is mandatory in UAE private schools regardless of the licensed curriculum, and the components that take time, script fluency and verb patterns, respond to short frequent practice rather than to intensive blocks. A pupil who builds those in primary rarely needs remedial Arabic alongside an examined course at sixteen, which is the expensive version of the same work and competes with examination subjects for time.

faqs.question: How many activities and tutors is too many for a Middle Years pupil?
faqs.answer: The honest answer is that sleep and unstructured time beat a fourth session, and that a tired pupil learns less in two hours than a rested one does in one. One tutoring session a week aimed at a named criterion, plus whatever the school sets, is a sustainable load for most Middle Years pupils. Families in this community have years in hand, which is an argument for patience and one measured target rather than intensity across five subjects.

faqs.question: When should we start thinking about IGCSE or Diploma subject choices?
faqs.answer: The subject decisions themselves land at the end of Year 9 and the end of Year 11, but the preparation that matters starts earlier and is not about subjects at all. Timed written work from Year 8, mark schemes read as instructions, and one longer planned piece a month make both transitions unremarkable. Tier entries for Cambridge subjects are fixed at an entry deadline months before the papers, so the structural decisions deserve attention a term before the school raises them.

sharjah/al-zahia.closingHeading: Ask for the numbers, then pick one target
sharjah/al-zahia.closingBody: Families in Al Zahia have the one advantage no examination-year household has: time. The way to use it is unglamorous. Ask the school for reading, spelling, number and criterion data rather than impressions, pick the single measure that is behind and not moving, buy a short block aimed at that one thing, and review it against the same measure in six weeks. Lessons run one-to-one over live video, no outcome is promised at any age, and every AED band here carries its source and month.

sharjah/aljada.tutorsIntro: The tutors below are the ones Aljada families most often need in a first term: bridging specialists who can take a child from one system's expectations into another, and board-specific tutors for candidates who have arrived part-way through an examined course.

intro.heading: A community that is still arriving
paragraphs: Aljada is one of the largest new communities in Sharjah, built out in phases west of the Muwaileh school belt, and its population profile is unlike anything in the older coastal districts. People here have mostly moved recently. Some came from another emirate, many from India, Pakistan, Egypt or the Levant, and a steady number from the United Kingdom or North America. A high proportion of its school-age children started at their current school within the last two years.

That single fact reshapes the tutoring conversation. In Al Khan the question is usually when a lesson can fit; in Muwaileh it is which component is losing marks. In Aljada the question is far more often whether a child who has just changed system is in the right place at all, and what has to be rebuilt before the current year can be judged fairly.

Changing curriculum is not a matter of catching up on content. A pupil arriving from a CBSE school into Cambridge IGCSE usually brings strong procedural mathematics and no experience of command verbs, extended written explanation or coursework. A pupil arriving from an American high school into the Diploma brings broad coverage and no experience of a two-year linear syllabus with internally assessed components. A pupil arriving from a British Year 11 into Diploma year one brings exam technique and a gap in the research skills the core components assume.

The second Aljada pattern is timing. Arrivals do not conveniently cluster in August. A family that moves in November drops a child into a Year 11 class halfway through a two-year course, often after the entry decisions for that course have already been made. Cambridge sets final entries months before the papers: for the March 2027 series, 27 November 2026 against an exam period of 3 February to 4 March 2027. A child arriving in December has already missed the window in which the tier could have been changed.

There is a social dimension too, and it affects how much tutoring a household can absorb. A child who has just moved is also learning a new building, a new weekend rhythm, a bus route and a set of friendships, in a community where many of the neighbours are themselves new. A schedule stuffed with four sessions in the first month tends to produce resistance rather than progress, which is why the plans that work here are deliberately light in term one and sharper in term two.

IB Gram handles this with one-to-one lessons over live video. IB Gram does not visit homes in the UAE, and in-home tutoring is a service run only in India. In a community still under construction that is a practical advantage as much as a philosophical one: the tutor pool does not depend on who has moved into the neighbourhood yet, and a family in a half-occupied phase can start in their first week rather than waiting for local supply to appear.

sharjah/aljada.programmesIntro: Four routes matter to families arriving in Aljada, and the useful information about each is what it assumes a new pupil already has. That assumption is where the gap sits.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: A two-year examined course taken in eight to ten subjects, assessed by syllabus or specification code, with tiering in Cambridge maths and sciences that caps the attainable grade. The course assumes a pupil has been taught to answer command verbs precisely and to write extended explanations that earn method marks.
programmes.countryNote: For a mid-year arrival the first job is establishing what has already been fixed. Which board, which code, which tier, and whether the entry has been made. A pupil placed into Extended tier on the strength of their previous system's grades, without the extended content having been taught, is the most common salvage job in this community.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects across two years with internally assessed components, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Roughly a fifth of each subject grade comes from work produced outside lessons across months, and the core components can prevent a diploma being awarded.
programmes.countryNote: A Diploma arrival mid-course is the hardest transition available, because the internally assessed work is submitted through a school with its own supervision records and deadlines. Ask the receiving school's coordinator, in the first week, which components transfer and which must be restarted. That answer determines the whole plan and is routinely left until it is too late to act on.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four published criteria, each marked 1 to 8, with the school converting the total into a 1 to 7 grade using boundaries it sets. There is usually no public examination at the end, so attainment is judged on tasks rather than on papers.
programmes.countryNote: Arrivals into the Middle Years Programme from examination-led systems often look weak in the first term and are not. Criterion-marked tasks reward process, reflection and investigation, which a pupil drilled for written papers has never been asked for. The reverse is also true, and both corrections take about a term.

programmes.name: System-to-system bridging
programmes.ageRange: Any year group, usually Years 8 to 12
programmes.description: Not a qualification but the work that actually needs doing: identifying which skills the new course assumes and which the previous system never taught, then closing those specific gaps rather than reteaching content the pupil already knows. Typically a defined block of sessions rather than an open-ended arrangement.
programmes.countryNote: Bridging is the most common first purchase in Aljada and the one most likely to be mis-sold as general tutoring. It should have an end point, a named list of gaps and a review date. If a provider cannot tell you which skills they are closing and roughly how many weeks it will take, they have not diagnosed anything.

sharjah/aljada.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects where a system change does the most damage, described by the specific gap a new arrival brings rather than by syllabus content. Lessons are over video, so availability follows board and level rather than neighbourhood.

subjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580
subjects.description: Arrivals from procedural systems are often strong here and still lose marks on structured multi-step questions and on the Extended-only content: functions, transformations and histogram density. Tier placement on arrival is the decision to check first.

subjects.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics 4MA1
subjects.description: Two papers with a formula sheet supplied. A pupil who has practised Cambridge papers must relearn pacing and question order, which costs marks for a term even when the mathematics is secure.

subjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625
subjects.description: The alternative-to-practical paper is where new arrivals lose most, because few systems teach control variables, repeat readings and systematic error as examinable content. It is a fast gap to close once named.

subjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620
subjects.description: Mole calculations usually transfer well from other systems; electrolysis conventions and the qualitative analysis tables usually do not. Those two topics account for most of a new arrival's deficit.

subjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610
subjects.description: The content is familiar and the marking is not. Examiners require the structure named, the process named and the consequence stated, and a pupil from a descriptive-writing tradition has to be retrained rather than retaught.

subjects.name: English as a second language and first language English
subjects.description: Summary and reading-for-detail questions reward precision over fluency, and directed writing has a form that must be learned. This is the subject where a confident speaker from another system most often underperforms in the first term.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The jump from a Year 11 examined course into Higher Level is real, and the exploration component is unlike anything most arriving pupils have produced. Early work on the exploration question protects a fifth of the grade.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: The scientific investigation is assessed on four criteria worth twenty-four marks, and a mid-course arrival often has no research question and no supervision record. That is an administrative problem before it is an academic one.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: A popular choice for arrivals because it feels accessible, and marks come from applying a tool to the stimulus organisation and reaching a defended judgement rather than from reproducing the tool itself.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: Up to three points together, with research and referencing conventions that examination-led systems rarely teach. Support is question framing and feedback on the student's own drafts; supplied text is a malpractice risk rather than a shortcut.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: New arrivals are usually placed in an Arabic stream by year group rather than by prior study, which can leave a child two phases from their actual level in either direction. Ask how placement was decided and when it is reviewed.

sharjah/aljada.regionsIntro: Aljada sits between central Sharjah and the inland school belt. These are the districts its families move between and compare with, described by the practical relationship to Aljada.

regions.name: Muwaileh
regions.note: Immediately east and the location of most schools Aljada children attend. Journeys are short, so Aljada pupils are available for an earlier evening session than coastal families, which widens the slots on offer.

regions.name: Al Zahia
regions.note: North-east, villa-based and a frequent second move for families who started in an Aljada apartment. School arrangements normally survive the move, so a tutoring slot set up here usually continues unchanged.

regions.name: University City
regions.note: Further east, the campus belt. Families arriving from abroad often look at both communities and end up in Aljada for housing while using the same schools and the same mock calendars.

regions.name: Al Qasimia
regions.note: West into older Sharjah, with long-established Indian-curriculum schools. A common first landing place for families who later move to Aljada once a lease ends and a school place is settled.

regions.name: Al Nahda, Sharjah
regions.note: North-west on the Dubai boundary. Families comparing Aljada with Al Nahda are usually weighing newer housing against a shorter commute into Dubai for work.

regions.name: Sharjah Garden City

sharjah/aljada.modesIntro: Three patterns fit a transition household, and the first of them has an end date. That matters, because an open-ended arrangement bought in a first panicked fortnight tends to outlive its usefulness.

modes.title: A defined bridging block
modes.description: A fixed number of sessions with a named list of gaps to close: command verbs, extended written explanation, practical write-up conventions, coursework expectations. It ends when the list is done, with a review rather than an automatic renewal.

sections.heading: Arriving in month four of a two-year course
paragraphs: The hardest tutoring problem in this community is not a weak pupil. It is a capable pupil who joined a two-year course after it started, in a system they have not been taught in, with decisions about their entry already made by a school that met them a fortnight ago.

Three things are usually already fixed on arrival. The board and specification, because the school teaches what it teaches. The tier, if the entry has been made, and Cambridge sets final entries months ahead of the papers, with 27 November 2026 the final entry date for a March 2027 series running from 3 February to 4 March 2027. And the placement year group, which is normally assigned on age rather than on prior attainment.

Three things are usually still open, and they are where the effort should go. Which subjects to prioritise, because a mid-year arrival cannot close nine gaps at once. Whether the tier placement matches what the pupil has actually been taught, which is a conversation to have with the head of department in the first month rather than the third. And how the internally assessed components will be handled, which in a Diploma transfer is the question that determines everything else.

The table below sets out what is realistic by month of arrival. It is deliberately blunt, because the most damaging thing a provider can do with a mid-year family is agree that everything is recoverable. Some things are not, and knowing which ones early is what allows the rest to be done properly.

sections.heading: The transition map, subject by subject
paragraphs: General advice about adapting to a new curriculum is useless. What a family needs is the specific gap in the specific subject, because the gaps differ sharply and some of them close in three weeks while others take a year.

The pattern that recurs most often is procedural strength with explanatory weakness. Pupils from examination-heavy systems arrive able to execute a method quickly and unable to say why it works, which is exactly what an explain question asks for. The reverse pattern arrives from criterion-marked systems: pupils who can investigate, reflect and present, and who have never sat a timed paper.

Language is a separate axis and is often misdiagnosed as ability. A pupil who has studied in English for years may still never have been taught the register an IGCSE directed-writing task requires, or the summary technique the reading paper rewards. That is a form problem rather than a comprehension problem, and it responds quickly to being named.

The map below gives the common routes into this community with the gap each one brings and a realistic length of support. The week counts assume one session a week with work done between sessions, and they are indicative rather than promises, because a pupil who does the work between lessons moves faster than one who does not.

Read the map as a diagnosis aid rather than a menu. The value of knowing that a Pearson-to-Cambridge move is a four-to-six session problem is that it stops a family buying a year of general tutoring for a paper-structure gap, and the value of knowing that a CBSE-to-Diploma move takes a full term is that it stops the same family abandoning the work in week five because nothing has visibly changed yet.

sections.heading: What follows a child between schools, and what does not
paragraphs: Families planning a move think about fees, uniforms and bus routes. The thing that actually causes academic damage is the assessed work in progress, and almost nobody asks about it until after the move is made.

Grades transfer as information and not as credit. A report from a previous school tells the receiving school something and binds it to nothing, which is why placement is usually made on age and on an internal assessment of the pupil. Examination entries do not transfer at all: an entry is made by a centre, and a change of centre means a new entry, subject to that centre's deadlines and its willingness to enter an external candidate.

Internally assessed work is the hard case. A Diploma internal assessment is submitted through a school with supervision records, authenticity declarations and the school's own deadlines. Whether partially completed work can be carried across depends on the receiving school and on how far it has progressed. The only reliable move is to ask the receiving coordinator, in writing, in the first week.

The practical lesson for an Aljada family planning a move or having just made one is to treat the academic handover as a separate task from the logistical one, with its own list and its own questions. The table sets out what to ask about each item and who holds the answer.

Ask for everything from the previous school before the final day rather than after it. Records become markedly harder to extract once a child has left, fees are settled and the contact there has moved on, and a complete previous record including internal assessment marks and predicted grades is the baseline a tutor needs and the evidence a parent needs if a placement decision looks wrong.

sections.heading: The Middle Years to Diploma step, which is a change of species
paragraphs: A large share of Aljada enquiries concern a pupil who was comfortable in the Middle Years Programme and is struggling in Diploma year one. It is worth explaining properly, because it is predictable and it is not a sign that anything went wrong.

Middle Years assessment is criterion-based. Each subject group is marked against four criteria, each scored from 1 to 8, with the school converting the total into a 1 to 7 grade using boundaries it sets. Tasks reward investigation, process, reflection and communication, and they are usually completed over days with access to resources. A capable pupil can score consistently well without ever having written for ninety minutes under time pressure with nothing in front of them.

The Diploma then asks for exactly that, plus a volume of content, plus internally assessed work that is genuinely independent. The grade drop in the first term is a measurement of an untrained skill rather than a collapse in ability, and treating it as the latter is how families end up buying content teaching the pupil does not need.

What works is narrow and quick: timed writing from the first week, mark schemes read as instructions, and the internal assessment question settled early so that the one genuinely independent piece of work is not also the first one. Eight to twelve weeks of that usually closes the gap, after which the pupil's actual subject ability becomes visible again.

It is worth telling the student this explicitly, because the first-term drop damages confidence more than it damages the final grade. A candidate who understands that they are being measured on a skill nobody has taught them yet behaves quite differently from one who has concluded they are no longer good at the subject. The second conclusion is the expensive one, and it is usually reached in about three weeks of silence.

sections.heading: Placed by age, assessed by attainment
paragraphs: New arrivals are almost always placed in a year group by date of birth. That is administratively sensible and academically blunt, and in a community with this much movement it produces two opposite problems that look the same on a report card.

The first is the under-placed pupil, usually from a system a year ahead in a particular subject, who spends a year revisiting material they know. The report looks excellent, nothing is learned, and the deficit appears later when the pace changes. The second is the over-placed pupil, dropped into the second year of a two-year course without the first year's content, whose report looks alarming while the actual problem is a specific set of untaught topics.

Distinguishing between them takes one diagnostic session with timed material from the current course. An under-placed pupil completes it comfortably and quickly; an over-placed pupil can do parts of it and fails specific topics in an identifiable pattern. That distinction determines whether the right response is enrichment, a conversation about placement, or a targeted content block.

The conversation with the school is worth having with evidence rather than impressions. Ask how placement was decided, what would prompt a review, and whether any internal assessment was used. Schools respond better to a marked script than to a parental opinion, which is the practical argument for buying a diagnostic before buying a term.

Accept that sometimes the answer is to stay put and enrich. Moving a child up a year group carries social costs that a report card does not show, and in a community where a child has just arrived and is still building friendships those costs can outweigh an academic mismatch of one year. Enrichment inside the current year group, with harder material and a faster pace, is often the better trade for a recent arrival.

sections.heading: What a catch-up block costs and how long it should run
paragraphs: Transition work should be bought as a block with an end date, which is a different purchase from weekly ongoing tutoring and should be priced and planned as one. A family that signs up for an indefinite weekly slot in a panicked first fortnight usually overspends and under-focuses.

On market rates, figures read in October 2026 put qualified online subject tutors at AED 150 to 300 an hour and IB or IGCSE specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above, with premium examiner-experienced tutors higher. In-home visiting rates run AED 180 to 350 in Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 rate table, and independent home tutors up to AED 500, because travel is absorbed in the rate. Monthly online packages of around eight sessions advertise from AED 799. None of those are IB Gram prices; IB Gram quotes after a consultation.

The planning number that matters is total sessions rather than hourly rate. A ten-week bridging block in one subject is ten sessions. Closing a Pearson-to-Cambridge paper-structure gap might be four. Rebuilding a Diploma internal assessment is three or four focused sessions plus draft feedback. Costing the block makes the decision concrete and makes it finishable.

Ask what the block includes and what happens at the end of it. A provider who expects the arrangement to continue indefinitely has a different interest from a family whose aim is for the child to stop needing it. The table sets out typical block sizes by transition.

sections.heading: Tutoring in a community that is still being built
paragraphs: Searching for a home tutor in a new development has a particular problem that older districts do not share: the local supply has not arrived yet. Tutors establish themselves where the population already is, which in Sharjah means the coastal districts and the school belt, and a newly occupied phase of a large community can wait years for that to catch up.

What families find instead is tutors travelling in from Muwaileh, Al Nahda or across the Dubai boundary, charging for the journey and available only at the hours the journey allows. For a pupil needing one subject at a convenient hour that can work. For a mid-year arrival needing a bridging block in two subjects within a fortnight, it generally does not.

IB Gram does not visit homes in the UAE, and in-home tutoring is a service offered only in India. Aljada families are taught one-to-one over live video, with screen sharing for papers and a shared whiteboard. The relevant advantage here is availability from week one in whatever subject and board the new school actually teaches, rather than whatever the nearest available tutor happens to cover.

The limits should be said plainly. Video sessions need a quiet room and a device with a camera, which in a household still unpacking takes arranging. A pupil under about ten usually needs an adult nearby at first. And laboratory bench time cannot be replaced on screen; a tutor teaches method, variables, uncertainty and analysis, and the school provides the apparatus.

sections.heading: The first fortnight after a move
paragraphs: The two weeks after a family arrives are worth more than the two months after that, because several decisions are still open in the first fortnight and closed by the end of the first term.

In week one, ask the school four questions in writing: which board and specification each subject follows, which tier the pupil has been placed in and whether the entry has been made, how the year group placement was decided and when it is reviewed, and which internally assessed components transfer. Those four answers are the whole basis of a sensible plan, and they are easier to obtain in week one than in week ten.

In week two, buy one diagnostic session in each of the two subjects that look weakest, using timed material from the current course. That distinguishes an under-placed pupil from an over-placed one and separates a content gap from a technique gap. Then agree a bridging block with a named list of gaps and an estimated length rather than an open-ended weekly slot.

Then leave it alone for a term. New arrivals are also adjusting to a country, a building site, a different weekend and a new set of friends, and a schedule stuffed with four tutoring sessions in the first month produces resistance rather than progress. Two sessions a week, a clear list, and a review against the first real school assessment is the shape that works in this community.

One final question to ask any provider before starting: what happens if the specialist you need is not free at your hour. Scarce Higher Level subjects sometimes have nobody available in a Sharjah evening, and the honest answers are a waiting position or a tutor in a time zone that fits. A generalist described as a specialist is the answer to avoid, and how a provider handles that question in week one predicts how it will handle everything later.

whyPoints.title: Transitions treated as their own problem
whyPoints.description: A system change is a skills gap before it is a content gap, and the gaps differ by route. Sessions target the specific untaught skill, which is why a Pearson-to-Cambridge move takes weeks while a CBSE-to-Diploma move takes a term.

whyPoints.title: Available in week one
whyPoints.description: Because lessons run over live video, an Aljada family in a newly occupied phase can start immediately in the exact board and subject their new school teaches, rather than waiting for a local tutor supply that trails the population by years.

whyPoints.description: A pupil arriving in February of an examined year cannot close nine gaps, and saying so is more useful than agreeing. Plans here name what is not being attempted, which is what allows the rest of the work to be done properly.

whyPoints.title: Blocks with an end date
whyPoints.description: Transition work is sold as a defined block with a named list of skills and a review point, not as an indefinite weekly slot. The aim is for the pupil to stop needing it, which should be the provider's aim as well as the family's.

whyPoints.title: The student's work stays their own

faqs.question: We have just moved to Aljada mid-year. What should we do in the first week?
faqs.answer: Ask the school four questions in writing: which board and specification each subject follows, which tier your child has been placed in and whether the entry has been made, how the year group placement was decided and when it is reviewed, and which internally assessed components transfer from the previous school. Those four answers determine everything else and are far easier to obtain in week one than in week ten. Then buy one diagnostic session rather than a term of lessons.

faqs.question: My child moved from CBSE to Cambridge IGCSE. What exactly is the gap?
faqs.answer: Usually not content. Pupils from procedural systems arrive able to execute methods quickly and unable to explain why they work, which is what an explain question asks for and what a mark scheme rewards. The specific gaps are command verb vocabulary, extended written explanation that earns method marks, and practical write-up conventions such as control variables and repeat readings. Ten to sixteen weeks of targeted work usually closes it, considerably faster if the pupil does the work between sessions.

faqs.question: Why did a strong Middle Years Programme student drop a grade in Diploma year one?
faqs.answer: Because the two are assessed differently. Middle Years tasks are marked against four criteria scored 1 to 8, completed over days with access to resources, and they reward investigation, process and reflection. The Diploma asks for timed written output with nothing in front of the candidate, across more content, plus genuinely independent assessed work. A first-term drop is usually a measurement of an untrained skill rather than a fall in ability, and eight to twelve weeks of timed writing closes most of it.

faqs.question: Does an internal assessment transfer when a child changes school?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it depends on the receiving school rather than on the IB alone. Internal assessment is submitted through a school with its own supervision records, authenticity declarations and deadlines, so whether partially completed work can be carried across depends on how far it has progressed and on what the receiving coordinator will accept. Ask that question in writing in your first week. A tutor can help rebuild the academic work but cannot move the administration between two institutions.

faqs.question: Can my child's exam entries move with them to the new school?
faqs.answer: No. Entries are made by a centre, so a change of school means a new entry subject to the new centre's deadlines and its policy on entering candidates. Those deadlines sit well ahead of the papers: Cambridge set 27 November 2026 as final entries for a March 2027 series running from 3 February to 4 March 2027. Ask the receiving school's examinations officer which entries are being made, for which series and at which tier, and get the answer in writing.

faqs.question: My child has been placed in Extended tier without being taught the extended content. What now?
faqs.answer: Raise it with the head of department immediately, with evidence rather than impressions. Have the pupil sit an Extended past paper under timed conditions, marked strictly, and take that script to the meeting. A marked paper showing which specific topics are missing is actionable; a parental worry usually is not. If the tier is right and the content gap is real, that same marked paper also gives a tutor the precise list of topics to close, which is the fastest version of this repair.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send tutors to homes in Aljada?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not make home visits anywhere in the UAE, and in-home tutoring is a service run only in India. Aljada families are taught one-to-one over live video. In a community still filling out, the local supply of visiting tutors lags the population by years, so what is actually available locally is usually a tutor travelling in from an older district, charging for the journey and offering only the hours the journey allows.

faqs.question: How many subjects can realistically be fixed after a February arrival?
faqs.answer: Two, chosen on recoverable marks rather than on which grades look worst. With a few weeks before a series, exam technique improves through repetition inside one subject, so spreading effort across five produces shallow work everywhere. The honest plan names what is not being attempted this year and leaves it to the school. That feels uncomfortable and it is the only version that produces a measurable change in the subjects you did choose.

faqs.question: My child seems to be repeating work they already did. Is that a problem?
faqs.answer: It can be. New arrivals are placed by date of birth, which sometimes drops a pupil a year behind where a previous system had them in a particular subject. The report then looks excellent while little is learned, and the deficit appears later when the pace changes. One diagnostic session with timed material from the current course settles it: an under-placed pupil completes it comfortably and quickly. Take that evidence to the school and ask what would prompt a placement review.

faqs.question: How long does a bridging block take, and what ends it?
faqs.answer: It depends on the route. A Pearson to Cambridge move in the same subject is often four to six sessions, because the content transfers and the paper structure does not. A CBSE to IGCSE move takes ten to sixteen. A Middle Years to Diploma adjustment takes eight to twelve. A block should end with a named test: two timed papers at target standard, or a school assessment at the expected level, rather than drifting into an indefinite weekly arrangement nobody reviews.

faqs.question: What does catch-up tutoring cost around Aljada?
faqs.answer: Market rates read in October 2026 put qualified online subject tutors at AED 150 to 300 an hour and IB or IGCSE specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above, with premium examiner-experienced tutors higher. In-home visits run AED 180 to 350 in Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table, and independent home tutors up to AED 500, since travel is absorbed in the rate. Monthly online packages of around eight sessions advertise from AED 799. The useful figure is the block total, not the hourly rate.

faqs.question: Will our previous school's grades count for anything here?
faqs.answer: As information, not as credit. A report tells the receiving school something about your child and binds it to nothing, which is why placement and tier decisions are made on age plus the school's own internal assessment. Request the full previous record anyway, including internal assessment marks and any predicted grades, because it gives a tutor a baseline and gives you something to point at if a placement decision looks wrong. Equivalency, separately, is a Ministry process handled outside the school.

faqs.question: How was my child placed in their Arabic stream, and can it change?
faqs.answer: On arrival it is usually decided by year group and by whether the pupil has studied Arabic before, and it is then often carried forward unreviewed. Since Arabic is mandatory in UAE private schools regardless of the licensed curriculum, a placement two phases from a child's real level costs a year quietly, because the report reflects the expectations of the phase they sit in. Ask the school how placement was decided, when it is reviewed and what evidence would support a move.

faqs.question: Should we start tutoring immediately or let a new arrival settle first?
faqs.answer: Start the diagnostic immediately and the teaching gently. The information you need, particularly about tier placement and assessed components, has deadlines attached, so week one is the right time to gather it. The teaching load is different: a child adjusting to a country, a school and a new weekend will resist four sessions a week. Two sessions, a written list of gaps, and a review against the first real school assessment is the shape that works in a community of recent arrivals.

faqs.question: Does equivalency change if a child switches curriculum part-way through?
faqs.answer: The requirement attaches to the certificate eventually issued, so what matters is the qualification your child finishes with rather than the ones they passed through. For the British track, the published guidance reported in July 2026 asks for five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no lower than grade E or grade 3, excluding Arabic and Islamic education, plus one A-Level at grade E or two AS-Levels at the same grade. A mid-course switch can affect whether five subjects are actually completed, which is worth checking on moe.gov.ae early.

sharjah/aljada.closingHeading: Get the four answers, then plan the term
sharjah/aljada.closingBody: An Aljada family arriving mid-year does not need a sales conversation; it needs four answers from the school about board, tier, placement and assessed components, and one diagnostic hour to separate a content gap from a technique gap. With those in hand a bridging block can be agreed with a named list of skills and an end date rather than an open-ended weekly slot. Lessons run one-to-one over live video, every AED band here is a market figure with its month, and the student writes every word of their own assessed work.

sharjah/best-ib-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below cover Diploma and Middle Years subjects for students in Sharjah and at Dubai campuses reached from the emirate. Judge any of them the way this page recommends: on the trial lesson, the written note it produces, and what they ask to see before teaching anything.

intro.heading: Nobody can tell you who the best IB tutor is. Here is what you can check instead.
paragraphs: The search you just ran has no answer, and the pages competing for it mostly know that. What they offer instead is a set of signals designed to look like proof. A star figure the provider calculated about itself. A review count that appears as one number in the visible page and a different number in the structured data behind it. A grid of school crests under a heading that implies endorsement, where no relationship exists. Tiered pricing in US dollars, a phone number with a foreign country code, and a claim about being in the top few per cent of tutors that contradicts a different percentage two sections further down the same page.

A parent cannot verify any of that, which is why it is there. What a parent can verify is narrower, duller and far more useful: what a tutor asks to see before the first session, what they say when asked which exact subject and level they have taught and in which year, what the trial lesson produces in writing, and whether the marks in the school's own markbook move in the direction the session notes predicted. That is an evidence chain, and it is available to any family willing to spend twenty minutes assembling it.

This page is the method rather than a pitch. The order matters, so work through it as a sequence. Start with the marked work, because a tutor who begins teaching before reading a marked script is guessing about your child at your expense. Establish a baseline you could show someone. Agree in advance what would count as progress, in terms specific enough to be wrong. Then set a review date and treat stopping as a permitted outcome, because an arrangement with no exit criteria is not a service, it is a standing order.

The Sharjah context sharpens all of this in one specific way. Diploma cohorts at individual campuses in this emirate are small, so the number of people locally who have recently taught your child's exact subject at the exact level with the exact option topic is genuinely limited, and the number who will say so when asked is smaller still. Vagueness about what a tutor has taught is the single most reliable warning sign available to you, and it is the one question that costs nothing to ask and cannot be answered with marketing.

Two things this page will not do. It will not claim that IB Gram is better than the alternatives, because that claim would be exactly the kind of unverifiable assertion the rest of the page tells you to refuse. And it will not publish a statistic about our own results, because a figure without a sample size, a date and a method is decoration. What we will do is describe what we send you, when, and what you should conclude if it does not arrive.

Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video. IB Gram does not arrange home visits in Sharjah or anywhere else in the UAE; a tutor travelling to a family's address is something we do only in India. On a page about evidence that has a practical upside: an annotated script from a shared screen survives the session, which means the record you are auditing is the actual work rather than a recollection of a conversation in a living room.

sharjah/best-ib-tutor.programmesIntro: What counts as evidence changes with the programme, because the assessment machinery changes. A middle-years parent is reading criterion marks; a Diploma parent is reading mark schemes and command terms. Judging a tutor means knowing which evidence applies.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Assessment is dominated by externally marked papers in the session UAE schools sit in May, with one internally assessed component per subject. The evidence available to a parent is therefore specific: marked school papers against published mark schemes, internal assessment drafts with supervisor comments, and the predicted grade the school submits for university applications.
programmes.countryNote: Sharjah Diploma cohorts are small at individual campuses, so a parent asking a tutor which option topics they have taught is asking a question with a short list of possible honest answers. A tutor who cannot name the option your child's teacher chose has not taught the course your child is sitting, whatever they have taught elsewhere.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Criterion-assessed work across eight subject groups, four criteria per subject, each marked out of 8. There are no mark schemes and no papers to read, so the evidence a parent can audit is the criterion-marked task with the teacher's rubric attached. A tutor who talks about percentages and test scores at this stage is describing a different programme from the one your child is in.
programmes.countryNote: Because the Middle Years Programme is a minority curriculum in Sharjah, families here are more likely than Dubai families to encounter a tutor who has never worked with criterion rubrics. Asking to see how they would mark one of your child's returned tasks is a thirty-second test with a clear result.

programmes.name: The Diploma core: internal assessment, Extended Essay and TOK
programmes.description: The components where the question of what a tutor may legitimately do becomes sharpest. All three must be the student's own work, supported by a school supervisor, with an authorship trail. Legitimate support is teaching, questioning and feedback on the student's own text. The evidence of legitimacy is the trail itself: dated drafts in the student's voice, comments rather than rewrites, and a supervisor who has seen the process.
programmes.countryNote: There is an operator ranking in this market selling finished internal assessments at a published four-figure dirham price. The consequence of that transaction falls on the student, not the seller, and it can cost a Diploma. A provider's position on this is the clearest single signal of what kind of organisation it is.

programmes.name: Retake and November-session candidates
programmes.description: The easiest case in which to judge a tutor, because the evidence is already complete. A student with a final grade and a set of component marks has a diagnosed problem, and a competent tutor will ask for the component breakdown before saying anything about hours. One who proposes a programme without it is selling a term rather than solving a problem.
programmes.countryNote: Retake candidates in the northern emirates must also arrange entry through a registered examination centre, with deadlines months ahead of the papers. Any tutor implying they can arrange or expedite an entry is describing something they do not control.

sharjah/best-ib-tutor.subjectsIntro: The question to ask about any subject is not whether a tutor knows it but what they say the marks are lost on. A specific answer is evidence of recent teaching. A general one is evidence of a syllabus summary read that morning.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: A strong answer names Paper 3 at Higher Level, the proof and calculus depth, and the specific failure of writing an answer without the method that earns the method marks. A weak answer says the subject is challenging and that practice is important. Ask which paper the student's marks are being lost on and listen for a number.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics, modelling and calculator technique. A tutor who has taught it will mention the graphical calculator explicitly and will have an opinion on the route choice against Analysis and Approaches. One who treats the two courses as interchangeable has taught neither recently.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: The useful question is which option or Higher Level topics the school has chosen, because the answer is short and checkable. A tutor who names the internal assessment's demands on independent variable control and uncertainty treatment is describing marking they have actually done.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Ask what proportion of lost marks they see as mathematical rather than conceptual, and why. A specific answer, with a named topic, is a recent-teaching signal. Physics is also a subject where Higher Level cohorts at Sharjah campuses are small enough that option experience is a genuine differentiator.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Command terms do most of the damage here, and a tutor who has marked Biology will say so unprompted. Ask them to explain the difference in expected response between describe, explain and outline, and judge the precision of the answer rather than its length.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy, evaluation and the internal assessment's three commentaries with their word limit. A tutor who does not know the commentary structure has not supervised the component, whatever they know about economics.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Case-study application and the internal assessment's research question. Ask what makes a research question unworkable in this subject; a tutor with supervision experience will answer in terms of data availability rather than in terms of interest.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1 unseen analysis, Paper 2 comparison, the individual oral and the Higher Level essay. The diagnostic question is what they would do with a student whose ideas are strong and whose Paper 1 marks are not, because the answer reveals whether they teach analysis or teach reading.

subjects.name: Arabic and Language Acquisition
subjects.description: Confirm which course and which level before anything else, since first-language and acquisition routes are different qualifications with different demands. Arabic at Higher Level is a thin market in this emirate, and a tutor's honesty about that is itself a signal.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Study recall, evaluation and the experimental replication at the heart of the internal assessment. Ask what makes a replication choice a bad one; the answer separates someone who has marked the component from someone who has read about it.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: The exhibition and the prescribed-title essay. Few tutors teach it, and the ones who do will talk about precision of claim and counterclaim rather than about breadth of reading. Vagueness here is common and relatively forgivable; vagueness combined with confidence is not.

subjects.name: Extended Essay across subjects
subjects.description: A supervision-shaped job rather than a teaching one. The test is what they say about the authorship line. Anyone who offers to produce, finish or heavily rewrite the text has told you everything you need to know in a single sentence.

sharjah/best-ib-tutor.regionsIntro: Proximity is the weakest signal on this page, and in Sharjah it is actively misleading. These notes are about what each area's families actually need, not about how far a tutor would have to drive.

regions.name: Al Majaz
regions.note: Mixed Sharjah and Dubai enrolment, so a household often needs two different sets of school evidence read side by side. The practical ask here is a single written read covering both children rather than two separate arrangements.

regions.name: Al Nahda
regions.note: Late evening availability is the constraint, which narrows the pool of tutors far more sharply than subject expertise does. Families here benefit most from asking about the 7.30pm slot before asking about anything else.

regions.name: Muwaileh
regions.note: Short commutes allow earlier sessions, and the local school belt means several families compare notes on the same campuses. Word of mouth is stronger here than anywhere in the emirate, and it is still not evidence about your child's specific subject.

regions.note: Academic households that ask harder questions than average and are usually the first to request the week-six review in writing. This is the pattern that produces the lowest wasted spend.

sections.heading: What a search for the best tutor returns, and how to test each claim
paragraphs: Run the search and the same handful of signals appear. A star figure with a review count, calculated by the provider about itself, occasionally with one number in the visible page and a different number in the markup behind it. A grid of school crests under a heading implying a relationship. A claim about belonging to a small elite percentage of tutors, sometimes contradicted by a different percentage elsewhere on the same page. Prices in US dollars, or no prices at all. A contact number with a country code that is not +971.

None of these is testable by a parent, and that is the point of them. The useful response is not cynicism but substitution: for each unverifiable signal, there is a question with a checkable answer. A star figure cannot be audited, but a request to see what a session note looks like can be met or refused within an hour. A claim about examiner status cannot be verified by you, but a question about which subject, which level, which option topic and which academic year has a short answer that a tutor either gives precisely or does not.

The table below pairs each claim you will meet with the test that replaces it. Work down the right-hand column before you pay anything. A provider who answers six of these cleanly is not necessarily the strongest teacher available, but they are an organisation that can be held to something, which is a prerequisite rather than a bonus. For the record, this page publishes no star rating and no statistic about our own students, because a figure without a sample size, a date and a method is decoration rather than information.

sections.heading: Six questions that separate a specialist from a generalist
paragraphs: These six take about ten minutes and they do more work than any amount of reading reviews. They are all questions whose answers are either specific or evasive, with very little middle ground, and the useful information is in the texture of the reply rather than its content. A tutor who has taught your child's exact course answers the option-topic question instantly and without being asked twice.

Ask them in order, because the sequence matters. The first establishes whether they have taught the course. The second establishes whether they read evidence before teaching. The third tests their position on assessed coursework, which is the single clearest signal of what kind of operation you are dealing with. The fourth and fifth test whether the arrangement will produce anything you can audit. The sixth tests whether they will tell you an unwelcome truth, which is the quality that matters most and is advertised least.

One note on tone. A good tutor will not mind being asked any of this, and several will visibly relax, because specific questions are easier to answer than vague expectations. A teacher who has spent years explaining where marks go would rather talk about that than about their philosophy of learning, and giving them the chance is in everyone's interest. If the questions produce defensiveness instead, that is itself the answer, and it has cost you ten minutes to find out rather than a term. The table sets out what a strong and a weak reply sound like for each, so that the judgement is about pattern rather than instinct, and so that a parent who has never read a mark scheme can still tell the difference.

sections.heading: The marked script is the only honest baseline
paragraphs: Everything else on this page depends on one habit: reading your child's marked work before anybody teaches anything. A marked Diploma script shows where the marks went, question by question, against a published mark scheme. That is a diagnosis rather than an impression, and it distinguishes between four different problems that all look identical from the outside. A student can lose marks because the content is absent, because the content is present and the command term was misread, because the method was right and unshown, or because they ran out of time and the last third of the paper is empty.

Those four need four different interventions. Absent content is weeks of teaching. A misread command term is a habit fixable in a fortnight and worth more marks than the teaching. Unshown method is a single conversation plus drilling. An empty last third is a timing problem that no amount of content revision touches, and it is the most commonly misdiagnosed of the four, because the student's own account of the paper is usually that they found it hard rather than that they ran out of clock.

Four marked scripts is the minimum that distinguishes a pattern from an accident, and more is better. Ask the school for them; they are your child's own work and most Sharjah coordinators release them through the student or the school platform without difficulty. Put them in date order with the mark schemes and read the lost marks rather than the totals. If a tutor proposes a programme without having seen any of this, they are pricing a term rather than solving a problem, and the fact that they may be an excellent teacher does not change that.
bullets: Absent content, misread command term, unshown method and poor timing look identical from a grade
A misread command term is the cheapest and largest available mark recovery

sections.heading: Internal assessment drafts: what a legitimate feedback trail looks like
paragraphs: The internal assessment is where a family's judgement about a tutor matters most, because it is the component where the wrong kind of help carries consequences for the student rather than for the provider. There is an operator ranking in this market selling finished internal assessments at a published four-figure dirham price. A student who submits purchased work faces a malpractice finding, and a Diploma can be withheld. The seller faces nothing. That asymmetry is the whole reason to care about a provider's position here before the deadline panic arrives.

A legitimate trail is recognisable and dull. The student produces text. The tutor reads it and responds in comments on the student's own file, dated, in the form of questions and teaching rather than replacement sentences. Where the structure is wrong, the tutor explains what the criterion rewards and the student restructures it. Where the research question cannot be answered with available data, the tutor says so early, which is the single most valuable intervention available on any internal assessment and the one most often skipped. The school supervisor remains the person who sees the process and signs the work off.

What that leaves behind is an auditable sequence: dated drafts in the student's own voice, visible comment threads, and a reflection the student can explain in their own words if asked. Ask any prospective tutor what they do with a draft, and listen for whether the answer contains the word rewrite. An offer to tidy, polish or finish is the same offer in politer language. The honest version sounds less helpful and is worth considerably more, because it is the version that survives a question about authenticity.
bullets: Comments on the student's own file, dated, never replacement text
Challenging an unanswerable research question early is the highest-value intervention
Tidy, polish and finish are the same offer in politer language
The school supervisor remains the person who signs the work off

sections.heading: The evidence file: what you should have at week four, six and twelve
paragraphs: A tutoring arrangement should produce a readable file, and the file should be agreed before it starts rather than requested once a family has begun to worry. The schedule below is what we write into a plan. Its purpose is to make the week-six conversation a reading rather than a negotiation, and to make stopping an ordinary outcome rather than a confrontation.

Notice what is deliberately absent from the early rows. No grade movement is expected at week four, because a reported grade lags the work by most of a term and anyone promising otherwise is describing something they cannot control. What should exist at week four is narrower and more useful: one piece of school work in which the targeted failure did not recur. That is the first real signal, it arrives early, and it is checkable by a parent who has never read a mark scheme.

The right-hand column is the part most providers would prefer not to publish, because it names what an absence means. If week four produces nothing, the student is not transferring the session into school work and more sessions will not fix that. If week six produces nothing, the diagnosis was wrong, and the options are a different component, a different subject or stopping. An arrangement that cannot specify its own failure condition is not measurable, and an unmeasurable arrangement is how a family arrives at the end of DP1 with a drawer of receipts and no record.

sections.heading: Predicted grades, and why they are not evidence of tutoring working
paragraphs: Families treat the predicted grade as a verdict, and it is not one. It is a professional judgement made by the school for a specific purpose, which is university applications, based on the evidence the school holds at the time it is submitted. It can be conservative by policy, it can reflect one weak mock, and it can change. A prediction moving up is pleasant and a prediction moving down is alarming, and neither tells you much about whether a tutoring arrangement is doing its job.

What a prediction does tell you is what evidence the school is weighing, and that is genuinely useful. Ask the subject teacher which assessments the prediction rests on. The answer is usually two or three specific pieces, which immediately identifies what the next piece of work has to do and gives a tutoring plan a real target. That is a far better use of a parent meeting than asking whether the prediction could be raised, which invites a defensive answer and produces nothing actionable.

The honest framing for any tutoring discussion is therefore to separate the two questions. Has the specific failure we diagnosed stopped recurring in the student's school work: that is answerable from marked evidence within a month. Will the final grade be higher: that depends on the student, the papers and an examiner nobody in the conversation has met. A tutor willing to be judged on the first question and unwilling to promise the second is describing the arrangement accurately. One who talks confidently about the second has told you that they will not be measurable on the first.
bullets: A prediction is a judgement made for university applications, not a measure of tutoring
Ask which two or three assessments the prediction rests on; that is the actionable answer
Judge tutoring on whether the diagnosed failure stopped recurring, within a month
A confident promise about a final grade is a refusal to be measured on anything checkable

sections.heading: The numbers you should refuse, and the ones worth asking for
paragraphs: A page selling tutoring will show you figures, and most of them are unusable. A satisfaction percentage with no sample size, no date and no method. A median tutor score. A proportion of students achieving a particular grade, where the denominator is undefined and self-selected. A star figure the provider computed about itself, sometimes appearing as one value on the page and a different value in the structured data, which is a mismatch Google's own structured-data policy treats as a violation and which several pages in this market ship.

The test for any figure is three questions. How many cases is it based on. When was it measured. How was it collected, and who was excluded. A figure that cannot answer all three is not a weaker figure, it is not a figure. That standard rules out most of what you will be shown, including anything we could put on this page about our own results, which is precisely why there is nothing of that kind here.

Some numbers are worth asking for, because they are answerable and verifiable. What dirham figure per session, and is any tax included. How many sessions in the proposed block, and what happens to unused ones. What is the cancellation window, and what does a cancellation cost each side. If the tutor becomes unavailable mid-term, what is the replacement arrangement. Does the tutor hold the MoHRE private tuition permit, which is issued free of charge for two years and therefore cannot justify a fee on your invoice. Those five answers predict your actual experience far better than any published statistic.

sections.heading: Verification a Sharjah parent can actually complete before paying
paragraphs: Three checks are available to you and all three are quick. The first is the permit. Private tutoring in the UAE runs on the MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced through Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, granted free of charge for two years, and covering teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's own service listing, Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, shows no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Ask whether the tutor holds it. Anyone tutoring without one is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published, so disregard any specific amount quoted at you.

The second is the conflict question, and it is the one families most often get wrong because the arrangement looks convenient. A tutor who teaches at your child's own school is a conflict that regulators treat seriously: the permit carries a code of conduct barring service to students affiliated with the tutor's own school, and ADEK's professional-ethics rules for Abu Dhabi private and charter school staff prohibit paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school. Convenience is not worth placing a teacher in breach of their own code.

The third is the regulator, and it is about the school rather than the tutor. Private schools in Sharjah are regulated by the Sharjah Private Education Authority, which regulates private education in the emirate and approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. Dubai schools answer to KHDA, Abu Dhabi and Al Ain to ADEK, and Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah to the federal Ministry of Education. A tutor who claims familiarity with your child's school should know which of those inspects it. And to be explicit about our own position: IB Gram holds no licence, accreditation, approval or partnership from SPEA, KHDA, ADEK, the Ministry of Education, the IB or any awarding body, and operates no office in the UAE.
bullets: Ask about the MoHRE permit: free of charge, valid two years, no fee justifies an invoice line
Never engage a tutor who teaches at your child's own school
