faqs.question: Can we get an IB tutor on Sharjah's east coast?
faqs.answer: Yes, over live video, including for Higher Level subjects the local market cannot staff. What is hard out here is finding a specialist who will travel: the round trip from central Sharjah to Kalba is well over two hours before any teaching happens, which means one booking fills a tutor's whole evening and the hour has to be priced accordingly. Online, the published band of AED 150-300 for a qualified subject tutor applies unchanged, because distance is not a component of it. That is the practical difference.

faqs.question: How far is Kalba from the nearest IB school?
faqs.answer: It depends on the year, because programme menus change, so the authoritative answer comes from the school and from SPEA rather than from any third-party list. What is reliable is the geography: Fujairah city is the nearest larger centre with more provision, and central Sharjah, where most of the emirate's school capacity sits, is over a hundred kilometres away across the Hajar mountains. Ask any school you are considering which subjects and levels are actually running this academic year rather than which appear in the prospectus.

faqs.question: Would a tutor really drive from Sharjah city to Kalba for one hour?
faqs.answer: Some will, and the price reflects it. A tutor in a dense district fits two or three bookings into an evening; the same evening spent travelling to the east coast yields one. For that to be worth a professional's time the single hour has to carry what three would have, which is why genuine quotes for this journey sit well above the published AED 180-500 in-home band. There is also a reliability cost: one road problem removes the session entirely rather than shortening it.

faqs.question: What do east coast families do about specialist subjects?
faqs.answer: Historically, one of four things. Board or stay with relatives on the western side, which solves the problem completely at the cost of money and a teenager's home life. Drive west weekly, which costs an afternoon and evening every week for two years and fails whenever the road fails. Use whoever is locally available and accept the specialism gap. Or rely on the school, which in a small cohort often gives more individual attention than a large one. Online specialist cover is the fifth option and the only one with no travel in it.

faqs.question: Is boarding in Sharjah city worth it for a Diploma student?
faqs.answer: It can be, and it is the most complete answer to a school that cannot staff a student's subject combination at all. It is also the most expensive in every sense: fees, accommodation and family separation during term, which is a real cost rather than a rhetorical one. The question worth asking first is narrower than boarding or not: is the gap the whole programme, or one or two Higher Level subjects. If it is the latter, online specialist cover addresses it without the student leaving home.

faqs.question: How does a private candidate sit IGCSE exams in the UAE?
faqs.answer: Through a centre, not individually. A candidate studying a subject their school does not enter has to find a centre willing to accept them for it, and that arrangement must exist before the entry deadline rather than before the exam. The boards publish their own guidance on finding a centre and on what private candidates may enter, and that guidance on the board's site is the authoritative source. For Cambridge, final entries for the February-March 2027 series were published as due 27 November 2026.

faqs.question: Which exam centre would a student in Kalba use?
faqs.answer: Normally their own school, if it enters them. For a subject the school does not enter, or for a candidate not enrolled at an entering school, the centre has to be arranged and the board's own centre guidance is where to start. One regional detail catches families: every Cambridge centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones, and Cambridge states it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, as it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam otherwise.

faqs.question: Does Kalba come under SPEA or the Ministry of Education?
faqs.answer: SPEA. Kalba and Khor Fakkan are part of Sharjah, so private schools here are regulated by the Sharjah Private Education Authority despite sitting over a hundred kilometres from the city and immediately beside Fujairah, whose private schools fall under the federal Ministry of Education. SPEA's remit is wide: the UAE government portal states that Sharjah's authority approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. Cross the emirate boundary and both the regulator and the framework change.

faqs.question: What happens if the school here does not offer the subject my child needs?
faqs.answer: Two separate problems have to be solved: learning it and sitting it. Learning it can be arranged with an online specialist, working from the board's syllabus and the student's own materials. Sitting it requires a centre willing to enter them for that subject, arranged before the entry deadline. Families who solve only the first find in November that the second was the harder one. Start with the entry question, because it has a fixed date, then build the teaching plan around the paper.

faqs.question: Is group tuition a realistic option on the east coast?
faqs.answer: For content coverage in a mainstream subject, yes, and it is the cheapest option per student. For a scarce specialism it usually is not, because a group needs several students at the same level in the same subject to exist, which is exactly what a smaller town lacks. The other thing a group cannot provide is individual script analysis against the mark scheme, which is the single most valuable use of one-to-one time. Decide which of those two your child needs before comparing prices.

faqs.question: How much extra does distance add to an in-home tutoring rate?
faqs.answer: Enough to change the nature of the purchase. The published in-home band of AED 180-500 an hour assumes urban conditions: a route, several bookings in one evening, and a journey measured in minutes. From central Sharjah to Kalba the round trip is well over two hours, which reduces the evening to one booking, so the hour has to carry what three would have. An east-coast quote is therefore either from a local tutor at roughly the published band, or from someone travelling at well above it.

faqs.question: Can my child study a subject the school does not teach?
faqs.answer: Yes, and students do, but it requires more organisation than families expect. The teaching can be arranged online with a specialist working from the board's syllabus. The exam entry has to go through a centre that will accept the candidate for that subject, arranged well ahead of the deadline. And the student has to carry the independent workload that a timetabled class would otherwise structure, which is the part that most often fails. It is a good option for a motivated student and a poor one otherwise.

faqs.question: Does a weaker internet connection make online lessons unworkable?
faqs.answer: Usually not. A one-to-one session needs stable audio and a shared writing surface, not high-definition video of either party, and turning video off during written work is normal rather than a failure. Use a laptop or tablet rather than a phone, use headphones, and sit where the signal is best rather than where the desk is. The board is saved as the session runs, so a drop loses nothing written. Where a connection is genuinely unreliable, a local in-home tutor is the sensible choice.

faqs.question: Are there enough Cambridge-trained teachers on the east coast?
faqs.answer: For the core subjects, generally yes; local capacity in mathematics, the sciences and English is usually sound. The thin areas are depth and breadth at once: Higher Level Diploma sciences, the quantitative Economics paper, Computer Science, and discipline-specific coursework supervision. That is a function of population rather than of quality, and it is the same pattern a smaller town shows anywhere. It is also exactly the gap that an online specialist fills without anyone having to relocate or travel.

faqs.question: What is the earliest we should plan for a scarce subject out here?
faqs.answer: The autumn term before you need it, which is earlier than families in the city need to act. Specialist calendars fill for the year, and the east coast has no local fallback to absorb an overflow: a Sharjah city family that leaves it until February can at least buy a local generalist as a stopgap, and a Kalba family often cannot. The published premium bands also rise in the eight to twelve weeks before a series, which is the market confirming the same advice from a different direction.

sharjah/kalba.closingHeading: The geography stops being the problem
sharjah/kalba.closingBody: Start with the school: which subjects and levels are running, and what support already exists. Then work out whether your gap is specialism or technique, because they need different purchases. Send us the board, level and syllabus code from the exam entry with two recent marked scripts, and we will tell you whether we cover that combination now, whether there is a wait, and where the tutor is based. The introductory session is at no charge, one per family, with the student present. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video, with no drive over the mountains on either side.

sharjah/khor-fakkan.tutorsIntro: The tutors below cover Diploma and IGCSE subjects for students in small east-coast cohorts, including the option-specific papers a generalist cannot teach. Each works from the student's own scripts and from the option their class was actually entered for.

intro.heading: A class of four, and the choices somebody made for it
paragraphs: Khor Fakkan sits on the Gulf of Oman, a Sharjah enclave on the east coast with the Hajar mountains behind it and Fujairah territory on either side. It has a container port, an amphitheatre cut into the rock, a corniche and a small, settled population. What it does not have is the kind of school market that exists ninety minutes away on the other side of the mountains. The private-school set here is small, and that single fact produces an academic problem almost nothing written about UAE tutoring acknowledges.

The problem is not teaching quality. East-coast teachers are frequently excellent and are often doing more than their counterparts in the city, because a school with one class per year group needs one person to cover several courses. The problem is structural. A Diploma subject taught to four students by a teacher who also teaches three other subjects runs differently from the same subject taught to twenty-four by a specialist. The pace is set by whoever is in the room. There is no second set to move into. And the choices built into the syllabus — which historical period, which geographic themes, which set texts, which regional option — were made once, by that teacher, and they are now fixed for your child.

Those choices matter more than families realise, because they decide which past papers are relevant. A student sitting Diploma History will answer a Paper 1 built entirely on one prescribed subject, a Paper 2 built on two world history topics, and at Higher Level a Paper 3 built on one region. Buy a revision guide by subject name and you may be revising the wrong continent. Hire a tutor who has taught History but not that regional option and you have bought a historian rather than an examiner for your child's paper.

The second structural feature is supervision. Internally assessed work — the investigation, the exploration, the fieldwork report, the Extended Essay — needs a supervisor with time. A teacher running four courses and a tutor group has very little of it, through no fault of their own, and the student is the one who absorbs the shortfall. This is the single most common reason a capable Khor Fakkan student ends up with a mid-band internal assessment mark on a piece of work that was genuinely their own idea.

On delivery, plainly: lessons for a Khor Fakkan family are delivered online, one to one, over live video, with the student's own work on a shared screen. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. On this coast that is not a compromise, it is the mechanism. A specialist in a particular Diploma option does not live in Khor Fakkan, and the live-video lesson is the only arrangement under which one teaches your child at all.

sharjah/khor-fakkan.programmesIntro: The programmes available on this coast are fewer than inland, and the practical differences between them are sharper in a small school. These four cover the enquiries we take from Khor Fakkan.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: Two-year courses examined by written paper and identified by a syllabus code. Several Cambridge subjects are tiered, so a Core entry caps the grade while Extended runs the full range. Some subjects also carry a choice inside them: Cambridge History, for instance, is taken through one of two core content options plus a depth study chosen by the centre.
programmes.countryNote: In a Khor Fakkan school the tier decision is made for a group rather than for an individual, because there is usually one set. That makes it worth raising early: a student capable of Extended who is placed in a Core set with the rest of the year group has a capped grade for a reason that has nothing to do with their ability. Ask in the autumn term, not the spring.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS, to a maximum of 45 points. Several subjects contain school-level choices: the prescribed subject and world history topics in History, the optional themes in Geography, the works studied in Language A, the regional option in Higher Level History.
programmes.countryNote: The Diploma is the programme most affected by a small cohort, because it has the most internal assessment and the most school-level choice. A Khor Fakkan Diploma student is likely to be one of a handful in their subject, sharing a supervisor with several other courses, revising from past papers that may or may not match the option their class was given.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria each, marked 1-8, with no percentages or raw marks. MYP 5 ends in the personal project, which is the first substantial piece of independently managed work most students produce.
programmes.countryNote: In a small school the personal project is where the supervision shortfall first becomes visible. It is also the best possible rehearsal for the Diploma internal assessments, so a Khor Fakkan family is better served by taking it seriously in MYP 5 than by discovering the same weakness two years later with a fifth of a Higher Level grade attached.

programmes.name: Cambridge International AS and A Level
programmes.description: Three or four subjects in depth, examined in June and November series. Option structures are extensive at this level: History, Geography, Literature and several others are built from choices the centre makes, and the papers differ accordingly.
programmes.countryNote: A Level is sometimes the more practical route on this coast, because the external-entry arrangements are better established than the Diploma's and because a student can concentrate on fewer subjects where specialist teaching is scarce. Whether a particular centre will accept an entry in a particular subject is a question for that centre's examinations officer.

sharjah/khor-fakkan.subjectsIntro: The subjects we are asked for from Khor Fakkan are often the option-heavy ones, because those are the courses where a general tutor is least useful. Each entry says what is assessed and where the choices sit.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: At Diploma level Paper 1 rests on one prescribed subject, Paper 2 on two world history topics and Higher Level Paper 3 on a single region. At IGCSE the centre chooses between two core content options and a depth study. A tutor who has not taught your child's specific option is teaching a different course.

subjects.name: Geography
subjects.description: The Diploma course combines a core with optional themes — two at Standard Level, three at Higher Level — chosen by the school, plus an internally assessed fieldwork report. Examined answers need named, dated and located examples; generalities score in the bottom band.

subjects.name: English Language and Literature
subjects.description: The works studied are chosen by the school from a prescribed list, so the Paper 2 comparative essay depends entirely on what your child's class read. Paper 1 is an unseen analysis and is option-independent, which makes it the component a tutor can always help with.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: In the current Diploma guides the papers carry 36% and 44% with the scientific investigation at 20%. In a small cohort the practical scheme of work is the part most likely to be compressed, which shows up later in uncertainty handling and data analysis.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Organic mechanisms, energetics and equilibrium carry most of the lost marks at Diploma level. The subject rewards precise language about which bond breaks and why, which is teachable in a one-to-one hour and difficult to drill in a class of any size.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Students revise terminology and then meet unfamiliar data about an unfamiliar organism. The examined skill is applying a known principle to a graph, and it is practisable weekly from early in the course.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level carries a third paper worth 20%, built from extended unfamiliar problems. In a school with one Higher Level maths set, that paper is often the least rehearsed component in the building.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Marks come from applying a named concept to the stimulus. The Diploma research project is internally assessed with a strict word limit and needs a real organisation whose information is actually accessible, which is harder from a small town than families expect.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Correctly labelled and correctly shifted diagrams carry marks prose cannot. The internally assessed commentaries fail when the chosen article has no identifiable economic mechanism, and in a small cohort nobody has time to check the choice before the student writes it.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Theory papers plus an internally assessed solution the student develops and documents. Students who can program lose marks on success criteria and evidenced process, which is exactly the part a stretched supervisor cannot read closely.

sections.heading: What a Khor Fakkan tutoring search is actually about
paragraphs: Enquiries from this coast arrive in a different shape from inland ones. Nobody here writes to ask whether a tutor can get to their address, because everybody already knows the answer. What they write to ask is whether anybody teaches the thing their child is doing. A Higher Level subject with four students in the set, a regional history paper, a maths route the school runs once, an internally assessed piece nobody has had time to read: these are the enquiries, and they are all versions of the same question, which is whether specialist attention exists for a student in a town of this size.

It does, but not locally, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. The number of people within an hour's drive of Khor Fakkan who have taught Diploma History Paper 3 on a particular region, or Geography with a particular set of optional themes, or Physics under the current guide, is realistically zero. That is not a criticism of the town; it is arithmetic. Specialists concentrate where cohorts concentrate, and the cohorts are in Dubai, Sharjah city and Abu Dhabi.

So the useful framing for a family here is not whether to buy tutoring but what to buy it for. Three things repay it reliably on this coast. First, option-matched teaching on a course where the option decides the paper. Second, close reading of internally assessed work, because supervision time is the scarcest resource in a small school. Third, Paper 3 and other end-of-schedule components, which get the least class time anywhere and almost none where one teacher covers four courses.

Three things do not repay it. General revision with no identified target, because the student's difficulty is usually structural rather than a knowledge gap. More past papers without marking, because volume without feedback teaches nothing. And content catch-up in a subject the student is actually fine at, which is what families buy when they work from a report card rather than from a marked script.

sections.heading: Somebody chose your child's option, and it decides the paper
paragraphs: This is the point of the page and almost nobody writes about it. Several of the most popular Diploma and IGCSE courses are not single courses. They are frameworks inside which a school makes choices, and those choices determine which questions a student will face. In a large school with three History sets the department discusses it. In a school with one set and one historian, it was decided once, probably years ago, and nobody has mentioned it to a parent since.

Diploma History is the clearest case. Paper 1 is a source-based paper on one prescribed subject out of several. Paper 2 draws on two world history topics out of a longer list. At Higher Level, Paper 3 is built entirely on one region — Africa and the Middle East, the Americas, Asia and Oceania, or Europe — and a past paper from a different region is of no use whatever. A family buying a revision guide called History, or hiring a tutor who has taught History, may have bought something that overlaps with their child's examination hardly at all.

The same logic runs through other subjects. Diploma Geography combines a core with optional themes chosen by the school, two at Standard Level and three at Higher Level. Language A courses are built on works the school selects from a prescribed list, so the Paper 2 comparative essay is specific to those texts. Cambridge IGCSE History is taken through one of two core content options plus a centre-chosen depth study. Cambridge IGCSE Literature in English rests on set texts the centre picks. In each case the subject name tells you very little and the option tells you everything.

The practical instruction is short. Ask the subject teacher, in writing, which prescribed subject, which topics, which region, which themes and which texts your child is studying, and write the answers down. Then buy nothing — no guide, no tutor, no past paper — that does not match them. This single piece of housekeeping is worth more to a Khor Fakkan student than any number of extra hours, and it costs one email.

sections.heading: Timetable blocking, and the combination nobody offered
paragraphs: A school with one class per year group per subject has to place those classes in blocks, and two subjects in the same block cannot both be taken. In a large school there are enough sets to resolve almost any combination. In a small one the blocks are the constraint, and a student who wants Physics and Economics, or a third science and Visual Arts, or Music and a second language, may be told the combination is not available without the reason being explained as a timetabling one.

This matters because subject combinations close degree routes. A student who needed two sciences and ended up with one because of a block has a narrower set of destinations than their results would suggest, and that outcome was produced administratively rather than academically. Nobody did anything wrong. But a family that understands the mechanism can ask about it in the term before options are chosen, which is the only point at which anything can be done.

There are usually workarounds, and they vary in cost. Some schools will run a subject as a supervised independent study where a student is capable of it. The IB offers a school-supported self-taught route for a Language A the school does not teach, at Standard Level. Some subjects can be taken through an external centre entirely, though the sciences are the hardest to arrange because of the practical requirements, and the IB Diploma has no general external route of the kind Cambridge and Pearson operate. And sometimes the honest answer is to choose a different combination and stop fighting the timetable.

The table sets out the conflicts we meet most often from small-cohort schools and what each one realistically has available. Confirm anything in the external or self-taught columns with the school's coordinator and the relevant board, because availability varies by school, by subject and by series.

sections.heading: What a class of four gives you, and what it costs
paragraphs: Small cohorts are not simply worse. A student in a set of four gets more of the teacher's attention in an ordinary lesson than any student in a set of twenty-four, questions get answered as they arise, and nobody hides at the back. For a motivated student with a good teacher it can be the best teaching available anywhere. We would not want a family on this coast to read a page about small-school limitations and conclude their child is disadvantaged across the board, because that is not what the evidence looks like.

What a set of four costs is calibration and range. With four students a teacher has no distribution to teach to, so the pace follows whoever is most visible — sometimes the strongest student, who makes the course look brisk, sometimes the one who is struggling, which slows everyone. There is no second set to move into when the fit is wrong. There is no bank of peer work to compare a draft against. And a student has no idea whether their essay is good, because their sample size for what a good essay looks like is three classmates.

That last point is more consequential than it sounds. A great deal of academic self-assessment is comparative, and students in small cohorts routinely over-rate or under-rate their own work by a whole band. The most valuable thing an outside tutor provides here is not teaching at all; it is calibration. One timed paper marked against the real conventions by somebody who has marked hundreds tells a student where they actually stand, and it is often the single most useful session in a term.

The practical consequence for a family: buy the diagnostic before the course of lessons. A student who turns out to be working at a 6 needs different support from one who thought they were at a 6 and is at a 4, and the difference is invisible from inside a class of four. We run that first session as a timed component under conditions, marked properly, with the band and the reasons written down.

sections.heading: Internally assessed work when the supervisor teaches four courses
paragraphs: Every Diploma subject carries internally assessed work and every piece of it needs a supervisor: somebody who reads the plan, asks whether the research question can be answered, checks the method is feasible, reads a draft and says where the criteria are not being met. In a large school that is a defined part of a subject specialist's workload. In a school where one teacher runs four courses plus a tutor group, the time does not exist, and no amount of goodwill creates it.

The student absorbs that shortfall, and the absorption shows up in predictable places. Research questions that are too broad, because nobody narrowed them. Methods that cannot generate usable data, because nobody stress-tested them. Evaluations that list limitations without stating their effect, because nobody asked the follow-up question. These are not knowledge failures and they are not laziness. They are what happens when a first draft is also the final draft.

This is where an outside tutor does the most good on this coast, and it is also where the honesty boundary has to be clearest. A tutor may read the published criteria with the student, read what the student has produced, say which band it currently sits in and why, teach the missing skill, and ask the questions a supervisor with time would have asked. A tutor may not become the author: no text for submission, no data, no graphs to paste in, no ready-made research question, no restructuring until the voice has changed. The work is declared as the student's own, and a tutor who crosses that line creates a malpractice risk the student carries.

Note the distinction in the table carefully. The supervisor's role is defined by the IB and cannot be delegated; the school signs the work off. What a tutor adds is reading time and questioning, which is a supplement to supervision rather than a substitute for it. We also keep a record of what was seen and said in each session, so that the school can be told if it asks — and on a small coast where everyone knows everyone, being able to show that record matters.

sections.heading: Practical work and the collaborative project in a tiny cohort
paragraphs: Diploma science has two components that assume a cohort: the practical scheme of work and the collaborative sciences project, which replaced the Group 4 project in the 2023 guides and asks around ten hours of every Diploma science student without being separately marked. Both are harder to run with four students than with forty, and both are the first things to be compressed when a teacher is covering several courses.

The practical scheme matters even though it is not directly examined, because the written papers assume the experience it provides. A student who has processed real data with real uncertainties answers a data-analysis question differently from one who has read about it. Where the scheme has been thin, the gap appears in the examination as a weakness in graph work, error handling and interpretation — which looks like a mathematics problem and is actually an experience problem.

The collaborative project has a different failure mode. It carries no marks of its own, which in a busy term makes it the obvious thing to drop, and a missing project becomes a programme compliance issue rather than a grade issue. Those are harder to fix late and they worry schools more than families expect. In a cohort of four there is also nowhere to hide: the project is a group task with almost no group.

What an outside tutor can usefully do here is bounded and worth naming precisely. We can teach uncertainty handling, graph conventions, error propagation and data processing as skills, using the student's own data from their own school practicals. We can coach the student's planning and time management on the collaborative project. We cannot run experiments, provide data, or do any part of the project that is meant to be the group's. The hands-on work belongs to the school laboratory and stays there; what we add is the analytical layer that the examination actually tests.

sections.heading: What specialist support costs from this coast, and what scarcity prices
paragraphs: Market bands in dirhams, read in October 2026, with the source behind each figure. These are market rates rather than an IB Gram price list: our own arrangement begins with a free consultation and a trial session, and the figure that applies depends on the subject, the level and how scarce the specialism is. We publish them because most pages competing for this search publish no price at all.

The relevant thing for Khor Fakkan is the top of the range, and specifically what it is paying for. A premium rate on a scarce Diploma option is not buying a better hour of teaching; it is buying the existence of an hour at all. When the number of people who have taught Higher Level History Paper 3 on a particular region is small, the rate reflects that scarcity. Understanding this changes how a family shops: the question to ask is not whether the rate is high but whether the person has actually taught the option your child was given, because a cheaper tutor who has not is worth nothing on that paper.

The corollary is that general subjects should not cost scarcity money. IGCSE Mathematics Extended, Diploma Biology Standard Level, First Language English: these are widely taught, the pool is deep, and a family on this coast should pay the ordinary online band for them. Mixing the two up — paying specialist rates for common subjects, or hunting for a bargain on a rare option — is the most common purchasing error we see from small-cohort families.

One further caution that applies everywhere but matters more here, where arrangements are often informal. A low rate frequently means somebody working without the private-tuition work permit that national rules require. That permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers categories including registered teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. The government states that tutoring without a permit attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no schedule of amounts is published, so no figure should be quoted to you.

sections.heading: The specialist question, answered for this coast
paragraphs: Families here do not generally need persuading that online delivery is sensible; they need to know what it does and does not do. So, plainly. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE — that is a service we run only in India — and on this coast the in-home market for specialist Diploma teaching is thin to the point of being theoretical. The comparison worth making is therefore not online against in-home, but a matched specialist on a screen against the realistic local alternatives.

There are three of those. The school's own provision, which for the option-specific papers is the only teaching available and is often good, but has no spare supervision time. A general local tutor, available for common subjects and of limited use on an option-specific paper. And nothing, which is what a great many capable students on this coast actually have for their hardest component.

Against that, a matched online specialist does three things that are hard to get otherwise: teaching on the exact option, close reading of internally assessed drafts, and calibration — telling a student in a cohort of four where their work actually stands. What it does not do is replace a teacher, provide laboratory experience, or put an adult in the room with a younger child who drifts. We say that rather than overselling the format.

The practical limits are worth stating too. A session needs a reliable connection and a quiet room, which on this coast is usually easier to arrange than in a city apartment. It needs the student to have their own work to hand, because the whole method is working on their material. And it needs a slot the household can defend weekly, which on the east coast is generally easier than inland because the school runs are short. Those three conditions met, the format does what it claims.

sections.heading: Academic honesty where everybody knows everybody
paragraphs: A small town changes the texture of the honesty question without changing the rule. In a cohort of four, work circulates. Students help each other, often with the best intentions, and the line between discussing an approach and sharing a paragraph is crossed casually rather than cynically. Schools on this coast know it and watch for it, and the consequences fall on the student rather than on whoever was being helpful.

The rule itself does not bend. Internally assessed work is declared as the student's own. A tutor may teach, read the criteria with the student, read what the student has produced and name the band it sits in, ask the questions a supervisor would ask, and teach redrafting. A tutor may not supply text, data, graphs, structure or a research question, and may not edit a draft until the voice has changed. A service that sells completed internal assessments — and some in this market do, at prices in the low thousands of dirhams — is selling a malpractice trigger with a student's diploma attached.

Two practices help in a small-cohort school specifically. Keep a record: we write down what was looked at and what was said in each session, and we will give that record to the school if it asks. And keep drafts dated, so that a student can show the progression of their own thinking if a question is ever raised. Neither is onerous, and both exist to protect the student rather than us.

There is one more boundary with a local edge. The private-tuition work permit carries a code of conduct that bars a tutor from serving students affiliated with their own school, and Abu Dhabi's authority has professional-ethics rules to the same effect for schools in that emirate. In a town where the Higher Level teacher may be the only person for miles who knows the course, the temptation to hire them privately is obvious. It is not available, and a teacher who agrees is putting their own position at risk as well as taking yours.

sections.heading: Starting from Khor Fakkan, and the two things worth buying first
paragraphs: The first call is a free consultation and we ask for four things: the subject and level, the option your child's class was given, the school's internal deadlines, and the most recent piece of marked work. The option question is the one nobody expects, and it is the one that most often determines whether we can help at all. A family who does not know the answer should ask the subject teacher in writing before booking anything, because it changes who we would put on the case.

Two purchases repay themselves first for a student in a small cohort. The first is a calibration session: one timed component under conditions, marked against the real conventions, with the band and the reasons written down. In a class of four a student has no reliable sense of their own standard, and buying that information before buying lessons prevents a term of work on the wrong thing. The second is a supervision block on whatever internally assessed piece is next due, because that is the component where the school's time shortage bites hardest and where close reading produces the most marks per hour.

On coverage: common subjects match quickly. Option-specific papers take longer and sometimes cannot be matched in a given term — a particular Higher Level History region, a specific set of Geography themes, a Language A built on unusual texts. We say so on the first call rather than offering a generalist who will teach the subject rather than the paper. Where no UAE-based specialist is free we offer one from the wider pool, delivering the same one-to-one online lesson from another time zone, disclosed before anything is booked.

And one thing to do this week regardless of whether you buy anything. Email your child's subject teachers and ask, for each examined subject, which prescribed subject, region, themes, texts and tier your child is entered for. Write the answers on the front of each folder. Every hour of study your child does afterwards is worth more, and on this coast that housekeeping is worth more than a term of general tutoring.

process.title: Establish the option before anything else
process.description: Ask each subject teacher in writing which prescribed subject, region, optional themes, set texts and tier your child is entered for. On option-heavy courses this determines which past papers are relevant and which tutors can genuinely help. It is one email and it changes the whole plan.

process.title: Buy a calibration session first
process.description: One timed component under conditions, marked against the real conventions, with the band and the reasons written down. In a cohort of four a student cannot know their own standard, and this is the cheapest way to stop a family buying a term of work aimed at the wrong level.

process.title: Then a supervision block on what is next due
process.description: The internally assessed piece with the nearest school deadline, read closely against the published criteria. This is where a small school's time shortage bites hardest, and where an outside reader produces the most marks per hour of anything on this page.

process.title: Review against evidence, then stop or continue
process.description: At the halfway point, sit another timed component and compare. The review exists to decide whether to continue, change the target or stop, and we will recommend stopping when the evidence says so. A standing arrangement with no review is how families overspend.

whyPoints.title: We match the option, not the subject
whyPoints.description: Diploma History Paper 3 is a regional paper. Geography rests on themes the school chose. Language A rests on texts the school chose. A tutor who has taught the subject but not the option is teaching a different course, and on these papers that distinction is the whole of the value.

whyPoints.title: Calibration is the thing a small cohort cannot provide
whyPoints.description: With four students in a set there is no distribution to compare against, and students routinely misjudge their own standard by a whole band in either direction. One properly marked timed component tells a family more than a term of lessons based on an impression.

whyPoints.title: We supplement supervision without replacing it
whyPoints.description: The supervisor's role belongs to the school and cannot be delegated, and the school signs the work off. What we add is reading time and the questions a stretched teacher cannot ask. We keep a record of what we saw and said, and we will share it with the school if asked.

whyPoints.title: Scarcity is priced honestly, and so are the common subjects
whyPoints.description: A rare Diploma option costs more because the pool is small, not because the hour is better. A widely taught subject should cost the ordinary online band. We tell families which of the two they are buying, because paying scarcity rates for common courses is the most frequent purchasing error we see.

whyPoints.title: Coverage limits stated on the first call
whyPoints.description: When no specialist has taught your child's specific option this term, we say so rather than offering somebody who will teach the subject and miss the paper. Where only a tutor outside the UAE is available we disclose that before anything is booked, including what it means for an east-coast evening slot.

faqs.question: Why does the syllabus option matter so much for a Khor Fakkan student?
faqs.answer: Because several courses are frameworks rather than fixed syllabuses, and in a school with one set the choice was made once by one teacher. Diploma History Paper 1 rests on a single prescribed subject, Paper 2 on two world history topics and Higher Level Paper 3 on one region. Geography rests on optional themes the school picked. Language A rests on chosen texts. A past paper, a revision guide or a tutor that does not match those choices overlaps with your child's actual examination very little. Ask each teacher in writing and write the answers down.

faqs.question: Can my child take a subject that no school in Khor Fakkan offers?
faqs.answer: For Cambridge and Pearson qualifications, often yes, through a centre that accepts candidates who are not its own students. Written-paper subjects such as Accounting, Further Mathematics and languages are the usual acceptances; subjects with a practical test are the usual refusals. Confirm with a centre's examinations officer before buying any teaching, because the entry deadline is the binding constraint and closes months before the paper. For the IB Diploma the answer is different: registration runs through an IB World School and there is no equivalent general external route.

faqs.question: Is a class of four students better or worse than a class of twenty-four?
faqs.answer: Both, in different respects, and it is worth being precise. A set of four gives more teacher attention per lesson than any large class can, and for a motivated student with a good teacher it is excellent. What it lacks is calibration and range: no distribution to teach to, no second set to move into, and no bank of peer work against which a student can judge their own. Students in small cohorts commonly misjudge their standard by a whole band. That is the gap an outside marker fills.

faqs.question: Why does my child's teacher have so little time for the internal assessment?
faqs.answer: Usually because they are covering several courses. In a school with one class per year group, a single teacher may run four subjects plus a tutor group, and supervision time for internally assessed work is the first thing that gets squeezed. It is a structural shortage rather than a failure of effort. The visible consequences are predictable: research questions nobody narrowed, methods nobody stress-tested, evaluations nobody asked the follow-up question about. That is exactly where an outside reader produces the most marks per hour.

faqs.question: Do your tutors travel to Khor Fakkan?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not run in-home visits anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India. Every lesson here is delivered online, one to one, over live video, with the student's own work on a shared screen. On this coast that is the mechanism rather than a compromise: a specialist who has taught a particular Diploma option does not live in Khor Fakkan, and the drive from Sharjah city across the Hajar range is a day's commitment for a sixty-minute lesson. Live video is how specialist teaching reaches this coast at all.

faqs.question: My child was told a subject combination is not available. Why?
faqs.answer: Most often it is timetable blocking rather than a judgement about your child. A school with one set per subject has to place those sets in blocks, and two subjects in the same block cannot both be taken. In a large school there are enough sets to resolve it; in a small one the block is the constraint. Workarounds exist and vary: a level change, a supervised independent study, the school-supported self-taught Language A route at Standard Level, or an external entry. Ask the coordinator the term before options close, not after.

faqs.question: Which authority regulates schools in Khor Fakkan?
faqs.answer: Sharjah's own authority, because Khor Fakkan is a Sharjah enclave even though it sits on the east coast with Fujairah territory around it. On the UAE government's own account that authority regulates private education in the emirate, and Sharjah's and Ras Al Khaimah's authorities approve tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. Schools in Fujairah city nearby fall under federal Ministry of Education supervision instead. If your child attends across the boundary, the authority that matters is the one licensing the school.

faqs.question: How much does an option-specific Diploma tutor cost on the east coast?
faqs.answer: Market rates read in October 2026 put an IB or IGCSE specialist at roughly AED 200-450 or more an hour, with premium named tutors published as high as AED 650. Those are other providers' figures, not ours. The important point is what the rate pays for: on a rare option it is buying the existence of an hour rather than a better hour. Widely taught subjects should cost the ordinary online band of AED 150-300. Our own arrangement starts with a free consultation and a trial session.

faqs.question: What is the collaborative sciences project and why does it matter here?
faqs.answer: It replaced the Group 4 project in the 2023 science guides. Every Diploma science student takes part, it asks around ten hours, and it carries no marks of its own — which is exactly why it is the first thing dropped in a busy term. In a cohort of four there is also almost no group to collaborate with. A missing project becomes a programme compliance problem rather than a grade one, and those are harder to resolve late. A tutor can help with planning and time management; the project itself belongs to the students.

faqs.question: Does online tutoring work for Diploma sciences when the practical scheme has been thin?
faqs.answer: For the part the examination tests, yes. The written papers assume experience the school's practical scheme provides, and where that scheme has been compressed the gap shows up as weak graph work, error handling and data interpretation. Those are analytical skills done on paper, and they are teachable on a shared screen using the student's own data from their own school practicals. What we cannot do is run experiments or supply data. The hands-on work belongs to the school laboratory and stays there.

faqs.question: What should I buy first for a student in a small east-coast cohort?
faqs.answer: Two things, in order. First a calibration session: one timed component under conditions, marked against the real conventions, with the band and the reasons written down. In a class of four nobody knows where they stand, and buying that information before buying lessons stops a term aimed at the wrong level. Second, a supervision block on whichever internally assessed piece is next due, because that is where the school's time shortage bites hardest. General revision with no identified target is the purchase that repays least.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help if my child's cohort is moving too slowly?
faqs.answer: Yes, and this is one of the clearer cases for outside support. With four students the pace follows whoever is most visible, and a capable student in a set calibrated to someone else finishes the year under-stretched rather than behind. A weekly session can run ahead of the class, go deeper on the examined technique, and work on the components the timetable never reaches — Paper 3, extended response, the unseen analysis. That is additive work rather than remedial, and students usually find it the most enjoyable kind.

faqs.question: How do we avoid an academic honesty problem in a cohort this small?
faqs.answer: Three practical habits. Keep dated drafts, so the progression of your child's own thinking can be shown if a question is ever raised. Keep a record of any outside help: we write down what we looked at and what we said in each session and will give that to the school if asked. And be careful with the casual version of the problem, which is classmates sharing paragraphs with good intentions in a group of four. The consequences fall on the student, not on whoever was being helpful.

faqs.question: Can we hire my child's own Higher Level teacher privately?
faqs.answer: No, and it is worth understanding why rather than just being told. The UAE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years, carries a code of conduct that bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school. Abu Dhabi's authority has professional-ethics rules to the same effect for its own schools. In a town where that teacher may be the only local person who knows the course the temptation is obvious, but a teacher who agrees is risking their own position as well as your child's position.

faqs.question: How quickly can you match a tutor for a Khor Fakkan student?
faqs.answer: For common combinations — IGCSE Mathematics Extended, Diploma Biology Standard Level, First Language English — usually within a few days. Option-specific papers take longer and sometimes cannot be matched in a given term: a particular Higher Level History region, an unusual set of Geography themes, a Language A built on uncommon texts. We say so on the first call rather than offering somebody who will teach the subject and miss the paper. Where only a tutor outside the UAE is available, we disclose that before anything is booked.

sharjah/khor-fakkan.closingBody: If you are in Khor Fakkan and weighing up support for an IB or IGCSE student, send one email this week. Then send us those answers with the most recent marked script and the next internal deadline. We will tell you whether a specialist in that specific option is available, what a calibration session would show, and what is genuinely worth buying. sharjah/maryam-island.tutorsIntro: The tutors below take most of our arriving-family enquiries: IGCSE Mathematics and the separate sciences for students joining mid-course, Diploma subjects for students arriving into DP1 from a different system, and Arabic as an additional language for children meeting the subject for the first time.

intro.heading: The arriving household on the Sharjah waterfront, and its first academic year
paragraphs: Maryam Island is a waterfront apartment development on the Al Khan side of Sharjah, the sort of address that fills with people who have been in the country for a short time. Apartment stock turns over faster than villa stock, waterfront stock turns over faster still, and the result is a resident mix weighted towards recent arrivals, young families and households whose employment brought them here within the last year or two. That demographic has an academic profile, and it is not the profile of a settled family.

A settled family's tutoring question is about a subject. An arriving family's question is about a translation. Their child has a report card from another system, a set of grades that may or may not mean what they appear to mean, and a new school that has placed them in a year group based on age rather than on what they have covered. The parent cannot tell whether a 68 per cent from the previous school corresponds to a comfortable position or a serious gap, and nor can the new teacher, who has met the student twice.

The second feature of arriving households is timing. Children do not move countries at the start of the academic year; they move when a contract starts. A student joining in January is entering an IGCSE course five or six months in, with content already covered and an exam entry already being planned. A student joining DP1 in November has missed the opening of six subjects simultaneously plus the start of the Extended Essay process. These are solvable situations, but they are solved by mapping, not by general catch-up.

The third feature is Arabic, and it arrives as a surprise more often than any other item on this page. UAE private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations, which is why those subjects appear on a British or IB timetable. A child arriving with no Arabic at all meets a subject their classmates have studied for years. Nobody warns families about this before the move, and it is one of the most common first-term surprises on the waterfront.

Everything below is organised around those three features. There are subject-level transition maps from the commonest previous curricula, a first-term plan week by week, a cost-in-context table for a household budgeting its first year, and a documents list for the administrative side. Delivery is one-to-one over live video, which for an apartment household means a laptop and a corner of a room rather than a spare study. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India.

sharjah/maryam-island.programmesIntro: For an arriving student, the question about each programme is not what it covers but what it assumes you have already done. That assumption is where the gap sits, and it differs sharply between programmes.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE
programmes.description: A two-year course with content distributed across both years and an exam entry made months before the papers. Joining in the middle means arriving after specific topics have been taught and assessed. The practical difficulty is rarely the total volume; it is that the student is sitting end-of-unit tests on material covered before they arrived, which produces low marks that look like weakness rather than absence.
programmes.countryNote: An arriving family's first question should be which board and which syllabus code, taken from the new school's exam entry rather than the textbook. Cambridge and Pearson split the same subject into different papers with different tiering and practical arrangements. For Cambridge, final entries for the February-March 2027 series were published as due 27 November 2026, so a January arrival in Year 11 lands after that window.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. The Diploma assumes a particular kind of prior schooling: independent reading, extended written argument and self-managed deadlines. A student arriving from a system that assessed mainly by examination and recall meets all six subjects demanding something they have not practised, simultaneously, which is why DP1 arrivals feel harder than the subject content suggests.
programmes.countryNote: Mid-DP1 arrivals need the school's internal coursework deadline list on day one, because the Extended Essay and the first Internal Assessments are already in motion. We take that list from the student's own documents. Specific IB session and results dates are not restated here; confirm them with the school's IB coordinator against the IB's own published material.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Four criteria per subject, each marked out of 8, converted into a 1-7 grade through a school-set boundary table. For arriving students the shock is not the content but the assessment language: a child who has only ever been marked out of 100 for correctness now receives separate criterion scores for inquiry, communication and evaluation. Criterion literacy is learnable in a few sessions and is the fastest early win available.
programmes.countryNote: Children arriving into MYP from a national curriculum often read their first criterion report as a collapse in performance when it is a change in measurement. Explaining the conversion to both the student and the parent is usually the most useful thing anyone does in the first month on the waterfront.

programmes.name: International AS and A Level
programmes.description: Three or four subjects assessed almost entirely by terminal written papers. For an arriving student the narrowness is an advantage, because catching up on three subjects is more tractable than on six. The disadvantage is depth: AS questions reward sustained analysis rather than recall, and a student arriving from a recall-based system can drop grades without having learned less than their classmates.
programmes.countryNote: For families thinking ahead to UAE universities, the published British-track equivalency route asks for five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no lower than E or grade 3, plus one Advanced Level subject at E or above, or two Advanced Subsidiary Level subjects at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not counted among the five. Verify your own case on moe.gov.ae.

sharjah/maryam-island.subjectsIntro: The descriptions below are written for a student joining part-way through, so each one names what a late arrival has most likely missed rather than what the course contains overall.

subjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580
subjects.description: Late arrivals most often missed transformations, the harder trigonometry and vectors, which tend to be taught early in Year 10 in many schedules. The gap is narrow and closes fast, but it affects every subsequent topic that assumes the algebra, so it is worth mapping before anything else.

subjects.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics 4MA1
subjects.description: A student arriving from Cambridge material meets different question shapes in the later sections and a different paper split. The mathematics is the same; the pacing and presentation are not. A single full timed paper in the first fortnight is the quickest way to see what actually needs attention.

subjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625
subjects.description: Arrivals often land after the electricity and electromagnetism unit, which is the heaviest in the course. The practical paper is a second, separate gap: students from systems without an assessed practical component have never written experimental method in mark-scheme language.

subjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620
subjects.description: Reacting-mass and mole calculations are usually taught in the first year and assumed thereafter. A student who missed them can follow lessons on organic chemistry and still fail the questions, because the calculation underlies everything. This is the most common single gap in mid-course chemistry arrivals.

subjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610
subjects.description: The defined terminology is cumulative and the mark scheme rewards exact wording, so a student who learned the same biology in different words scores below their understanding. Rebuilding the vocabulary to the syllabus wording is unglamorous and quick.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: A DP1 arrival has usually missed the opening work on functions and proof, which the rest of the course rests on. Students from systems where proof was never assessed find this the hardest adjustment, and it is worth addressing directly rather than hoping it resolves with exposure.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Technology use is assessed, so a student arriving from a system that discouraged calculators has a specific, learnable gap in statistical functions and modelling tools. It is one of the fastest catch-ups in the Diploma because the content is not the obstacle.

subjects.name: IB Chemistry
subjects.description: The Internal Assessment is normally introduced in DP1, so a mid-year arrival meets both the content gap and a coursework process already underway. We prioritise getting the investigation topic agreed, because a late start there costs more than a missed unit.

subjects.name: IB Biology
subjects.description: Terminology volume plus data-handling technique, both cumulative. Arrivals who studied biology descriptively rather than quantitatively need graph and data-interpretation practice before content revision, because that is where the papers award marks.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The hardest subject to join late, because the course works through set texts and a student cannot retroactively read and discuss what the class has analysed. Guided analysis of unseen texts, however, is a transferable skill and the sensible first focus for an arrival.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: For a child meeting Arabic for the first time, the useful early target is script, high-frequency vocabulary and the specific material the school is using, since schools must work within the Ministry's framework for these subjects. Short weekly sessions work better than long ones.

subjects.name: UAE Social Studies and Moral Education
subjects.description: Content-light but unfamiliar, and taught in a different language of instruction depending on the student's stream. Arriving students usually need orientation rather than tutoring, and a few sessions settles it before it becomes a report-card issue.

sharjah/maryam-island.regionsIntro: Arriving families tend to look at several Sharjah neighbourhoods before choosing, and many move again within the emirate in the first two years. These are the areas that come up most alongside the waterfront developments.

regions.name: Al Khan
regions.note: The surrounding district, coastal and mixed between apartment towers and older villas. Many arriving households start here and it has the shortest run to the central Sharjah schools and to the Dubai boundary.

regions.name: Al Majaz
regions.note: Central, apartment-dominated and popular with new arrivals for its proximity to everything. A high share of children here commute into Dubai schools, which affects both school choice and the evening timetable.

regions.name: Al Qasba and Al Taawun
regions.note: Dense towers close to the Dubai boundary, with a transient resident mix and strong demand for IGCSE support. Students here attend a wide spread of schools, so the syllabus code matters more than the neighbourhood.

regions.name: Al Nahda, Sharjah
regions.note: Right on the Dubai line and heavily built up, with the longest cross-border school commutes in the emirate. Arriving families often choose it precisely to keep a Dubai school option open.

regions.name: Aljada
regions.note: A newer mixed-use community with schooling on site, which appeals to arriving families who want to reduce the school run in their first year. Demand skews to primary and lower MYP.

regions.name: Al Zahia
regions.note: Townhouses and apartments with good access to the University City Road schools. A common second move for families who started in a central tower and want more space.

regions.name: Muwaileh
regions.note: The emirate's densest school cluster. Arriving families frequently end up with a school here regardless of where they live, which makes the afternoon return journey the main scheduling constraint.

schoolClusters.city: Central and coastal Sharjah schools
schoolClusters.note: These are the schools arriving waterfront families most often shortlist, because they are reachable from the Al Khan side without crossing the city. Curriculum menus and available year-group places change constantly, so ask the school directly about mid-year entry before assuming a place exists.
schools: Our Own English High School, Sharjah

schoolClusters.city: Muwaileh and University City schools
schoolClusters.note: The larger and more varied cluster, generally with more curriculum choice but a longer run from the waterfront. Families comparing a mid-year place here against a closer school should weigh the return journey, because it sets the earliest workable lesson time for the next two years.
schools: The American School of Creative Science, Sharjah

sharjah/maryam-island.modesIntro: Three formats cover the arriving household's first year. The first two are time-limited by design, because a transition is a project with an end rather than an ongoing commitment.

modes.title: Transition mapping block
modes.description: Four to six sessions whose only purpose is to establish, subject by subject, what the student has covered, what the new course assumed, and what the actual gap is. The output is a written map a parent can take to the new school, naming topics rather than impressions. Most families find the gap is narrower and more specific than feared, and that two subjects need work rather than six.

Produces a topic-level gap list, not a general assessment
Usable in a conversation with the new school
Time-limited: it ends when the map is done

modes.title: Catch-up on one or two named subjects
modes.description: Weekly or twice-weekly sessions on the subjects the map identified, aimed at closing specific topics rather than re-teaching a course. Because the target is a list of named topics, progress is visible and the end point is defined. For most mid-course arrivals this runs for a term rather than a year, and it steps down to a single maintenance slot once the gaps close.

One or two subjects only, chosen by the size of the gap

modes.title: Arabic from the beginning
modes.description: Short, frequent sessions for a child meeting Arabic for the first time, working with the material the school is actually using rather than a parallel syllabus, since schools must stay within the Ministry's framework for these subjects. The target in year one is script, high-frequency vocabulary and classroom survival rather than fluency, which is a realistic goal and a measurable one.

Built on the school's own material and stream

sections.heading: What a Maryam Island tutoring search is usually asking for
paragraphs: Searches from waterfront addresses in Sharjah skew towards two phrases: a tutor for a specific subject, and help catching up. The second is the more honest description of what is wanted, and it is also the harder brief, because catching up is not a subject. Before any teaching happens, somebody has to establish what the student has actually covered and what the new course assumed they had, and those two lists are rarely compared by anyone.

The reason nobody compares them is that no single person holds both. The previous school knows what it taught and no longer has the student. The new school knows its own scheme of work and has met the student twice. The parent has a report card in a different format. The student, asked what they have covered, will reasonably say they do not know, because syllabus structure is not something students track. A tutor working across both is the only party positioned to build the comparison.

That is why the first product on this page is a map rather than a course. Four to six sessions working from the previous school's syllabus, the old reports and the new scheme of work produces a topic-level list of what is genuinely missing. In our experience that list is usually shorter and more specific than parents expect - two or three topics in two subjects rather than a general deficit - and it converts an anxious open-ended worry into a finite piece of work.

Because lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video, an arriving family does not need to solve the logistics of a stranger visiting an apartment they have barely unpacked, and does not need a spare room. A laptop, a quiet corner and headphones is the whole requirement. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; that is a service we run only in India, and we would rather state it here than let you discover it later.
bullets: Catching up is not a subject; it needs a topic-level comparison first
No single party holds both the old syllabus and the new scheme of work
A mapping block normally finds a shorter, more specific gap than feared

sections.heading: The curriculum transition map, subject by subject
paragraphs: The table below sets out the commonest transitions into Sharjah schools and what each one actually requires. It is deliberately organised by where the student is coming from rather than by subject, because the gap depends almost entirely on the previous system's assessment style. A student arriving from a curriculum that tested recall needs technique; one arriving from a curriculum that tested extended writing needs content.

Read the fourth column carefully, because it is where families most often misjudge. The gap to close is usually not a list of topics; it is a mode of assessment. A student moving from a national curriculum into IGCSE frequently knows more content than their classmates and scores lower, because the questions ask for applied reasoning rather than reproduction. Teaching that student more content is the intuitive response and the wrong one.

The fifth column gives the support period we typically see, and it is shorter than families assume. Most transitions settle inside a term when they are mapped properly at the start. The transitions that take longer are the ones involving a new language of instruction, or a move into the Diploma from a system with no independent-research component, because those involve building a working habit rather than filling a gap.

One structural caution. A mid-year arrival into Year 11 or DP2 is a different proposition from one into Year 10 or DP1, because the exam entry and the coursework schedule are already fixed. For Cambridge candidates, final entries for the February-March 2027 series were published as due 27 November 2026, so a January arrival inherits the entry decisions the previous school or the new one has already made.

sections.heading: The first term, week by week
paragraphs: Arriving families usually try to solve everything in the first fortnight and then lose momentum. A sequenced first term works better, because the information needed to make good decisions does not exist on day one. The table below sets out the order we use, and the logic is simple: gather, map, target, then commit. Nothing irreversible should be bought in weeks one to three.

Weeks one and two are for watching. The student is adjusting socially as much as academically, and the first pieces of marked work are not yet reliable indicators of anything. What is worth doing in this window is administrative: getting the school's scheme of work, the syllabus codes from the exam entry, the internal coursework deadline list if the student is in the Diploma, and the previous school's final reports in a readable form.

Weeks three to six are the mapping window. By this point there is real marked work, the student has a view about which lessons are confusing, and a tutor can compare the two syllabuses meaningfully. This is where the four-to-six-session mapping block belongs. The output should be a short written document naming the topics, because a map in somebody's memory is not useful at the parent meeting in week eight.

From week seven onwards the work is targeted and measurable, and the quantity should fall rather than rise. A household that is still buying four sessions a week in March for a student who arrived in January has either misjudged the gap or never mapped it. The honest end state for most transitions is one weekly session in one subject, and then nothing.

sections.heading: Arabic, social studies and the subjects nobody mentioned before the move
paragraphs: Families relocating to the UAE research schools, fees and curricula thoroughly and almost never discover in advance that their child will study Arabic. The basis is federal: private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. So a British or IB timetable in Sharjah carries those subjects alongside everything the board requires.

Dubai's regulator publishes the most detailed account of how this works, and it is useful reading even for a Sharjah family because it shows the mechanics. KHDA calculates mandatory-subject instructional time on a 40-minute lesson unit, permits schools to vary lesson length provided total weekly time is met, and advises that any mandatory-subject lesson should be at least 25 minutes. It also requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, stating that combined classes are strictly prohibited.

For an arriving child the practical consequence is that the stream matters more than the subject name. Arabic as a first language and Arabic as an additional language are different courses with different expectations, and a newly arrived non-Arabic speaker placed correctly in the additional-language stream has a manageable task. The content is also controlled: KHDA states that for these subjects the use of any different or additional content, without prior permission from the Ministry, is strictly prohibited, so support means working with the school's own material.

The sensible year-one target is not fluency. It is script, high-frequency vocabulary and the ability to follow the lesson, which is achievable with thirty to forty-five minutes two or three times a week. Families who attempt an intensive Arabic programme alongside an IGCSE catch-up in the same term usually abandon both. And for anyone planning ahead to equivalency: Arabic and Islamic education are not counted among the five required subjects on the British track, which removes one source of pressure.

sections.heading: Lessons in an apartment, and why the format suits a tower address
paragraphs: A practical section, because it is a real question on the waterfront and nobody writes about it. Apartment living changes the logistics of tutoring in ways a villa does not. There is usually no spare study. There may be a sibling doing homework at the same table. Sound carries. A visiting tutor means a stranger in a small shared space, at a time when the household is probably still unpacking and the building may still be filling.

One-to-one over live video resolves most of that quietly. The requirement is a laptop or tablet, a stable connection, headphones and a chair facing away from the room's traffic. Headphones matter more than the room does: they remove the sibling, the television and the lift lobby in one step, and they let the student speak at normal volume without the household listening. Families who set this up properly in week one rarely revisit it.

The second practical advantage for an arriving household is that the written record survives the chaos of a move. The shared board and the annotated work from each session are saved, so a student who is still finding their books can go back to a worked solution from three weeks ago. In a period when physical notes are frequently in a box somewhere, that is more useful than it sounds.

The comparison table below sets out the trade honestly, including where in-home provision is genuinely better. We would rather describe the real difference than claim the formats are identical. For a younger child in an unfamiliar country, an adult in the room has value, and our answer is to change the session shape - shorter, more frequent, parent within earshot - rather than to argue the point.
